messages.subject: Re: scale_fill_manual to create a custom legend : appears to do nothing.
messages.subject_clean: scale_fill_manual to create a custom legend : appears to do nothing.
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Try this:

library('reshape2')
library('ggplot2')

### Starting from your input data frame DSTest...

DSm <- melt(DSTest, id = 'Weeks')
ggplot(DSm, aes(x = Weeks, y = value, colour = variable)) +
    geom_point() + geom_line(aes(group = variable)) +
    scale_colour_manual(breaks = levels(DSm$variable),
                        values = c('red', 'green', 'blue'))

Look at DSm carefully and observe that the reshape of your data from
wide format to long makes it easier to define a color aesthetic with
the factor 'variable' that can be applied to both points and lines
simultaneously. Then it's easy to apply scale_colour_manual to the
levels of the constructed factor variable. More inline.

On Fri, Mar 9, 2012 at 1:38 PM, hamamelis <hama...@ntlworld.com> wrote:
> I am trying to create a custom legend. The following produces a legend with
> the labels called "red", "green" & "blue". I wish to replace them with my
> own labels like "No Risk Mean". scale_fill_manual appears to do nothing.
> What should I be doing?
>
> Thanks for any help, Ian
>
> Here is a description of my two Examples which follow the data preparation:
>
> Example 1: produces a legend box, but scale_fill_manual does not change this
> to my values; it seems to do nothing.
> Example 2 produces no legend and scale_manual_fill does nothing.
> I need to use geom_line & geom_point to see the case that has only a single
> date entry (WellbeM, blue) which will produce no line without geom_point.
>
> ### Prepare and read Input Data #############################
> DSString <-
> "Weeks, NoRiskM, FunctM, WellbeM
> 1, 2, 2.5, 1
> 2, 1, 1.5,
> 3, 1.2, 1.7, "
> DSString
> DSTest <- read.csv( textConnection(DSString))
> DSTest
> # library(ggplot2)
>
> ### Example 1 uses plDSTest2 ##############################################
> plDSTest2 <- ggplot(DSTest, aes(x=Weeks)) +
> geom_point(aes(y = NoRiskM,colour="red")) +
> geom_line(aes( y = NoRiskM,colour="red" )) +
> geom_point(aes(y = FunctM,colour="green")) +
> geom_line(aes(y = FunctM,colour="green")) +
> geom_point(aes(y = WellbeM,colour="blue")) +
> geom_line(aes(y = WellbeM,colour="blue"))

What you're attempting to do here is to create a color aesthetic on
the fly, using red, green and blue as the names of the levels of the
factor being constructed with the multiple lines of code. However, you
then try to redefine the colors by using scale_fill_manual() rather
than scale_colour_manual(). That won't work. As someone who struggled
with scales when first learning ggplot2, I feel your pain...

Consult the examples on pp. 108-109 of the ggplot2 book to see how to
do this correctly; if you don't have a copy available, then the
relevant code from Chapter 6 is shown below. Take note of the
differences among the three graphs and make sure you understand why
they are different, because they illustrate the fundamental concepts
of mapping vs. setting  a plot aesthetic. (Notice that only the
x-variable year is defined as an aesthetic in the ggplot() statement;
this is because the 'y' will vary in different calls to geom_line().
Aesthetics defined in ggplot() are expected to be the same in all
layers created by different geom calls.)

huron <- data.frame(year = 1875:1972, level = LakeHuron)
ggplot(huron, aes(year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level - 5), colour = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = level + 5), colour = "red")

ggplot(huron, aes(year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level - 5, colour = "below")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level + 5, colour = "above"))

ggplot(huron, aes(year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level - 5, colour = "below")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = level + 5, colour = "above")) +
  scale_colour_manual("Direction",
    c("below" = "blue", "above" = "red"))

>
> plDSTest2
>
> plDSTest2 + scale_fill_manual(
> #values=c("red", "green", "blue"),
> name="Means ",
> labels=c("No Risk Mean", "Function Mean", "Wellbeing Mean"),
> breaks=c("NoRiskM", "FunctM", "WellbeM")
> )
>
> ### Example 2 uses plDSTest1
> ################################################
> plDSTest1 <- ggplot(DSTest, aes(x=Weeks)) +
> geom_point(colour="red",aes(y = NoRiskM)) +
> geom_line(colour="red", aes( y = NoRiskM )) +
> geom_point(colour="green",aes(y = FunctM)) +
> geom_line(colour="green",aes(y = FunctM)) + ## colour = label for lines
> geom_point(colour="blue",aes(y = WellbeM)) +
> geom_line(colour="blue",aes(y = WellbeM))

In this case, you're setting colors for each variable rather than
mapping them, so no legend will be created because legends are only
drawn from *mapped* aesthetics**. You get the graph you want, but not
the legend, and trying to create it with the ensuing code will be a
futile exercise.

The code from the book shows you how to correctly define a factor for
an aesthetic on the fly - note that the aesthetic used in the manual
scale must match the aesthetic you created (in your case, color rather
than fill). A simpler way to do things, once you know how, is to
reshape the data first. Quite often, rearranging the data prior to
invoking ggplot() or qplot() can save a lot of time and frustration.

** A single value associated with an aesthetic is said to be 'set';
this is done outside the aes() call inside ggplot() or a geom. A
variable associated with an aesthetic is said to be 'mapped' (i.e., a
1-1 mathematical relationship) and is defined inside an aes() call. In
order for a legend to be drawn, an aesthetic has to be mapped. This is
a fundamental concept in ggplot2 which has to be grasped; otherwise,
you're in for a lot of frustration.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: position="dodge" not working with geom_text in 0.90?
messages.subject_clean: position="dodge" not working with geom_text in 0.90?
messages.body_plain:
I couldn't get your code to dodge the text in 0.8.9, until I changed the code from position="dodge" to position=position_dodge(0.9). This is probably because text objects are treated like points, and don't have a real width/height.

After making that change to your code, I tracked down where the change in behavior happened... it looks like it happened with this commit:
  https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/commit/ac91fe4

I believe the change is actually a feature, not a bug. :)

Typically, a variable is mapped to fill or colour, and each level of that variable indicates a separate group. (Actually, all the discrete variables are crossed to form the groups, but that's not important here.) Next, all objects that have the same x position, but are in different groups, get dodged.

With the geom_bar, 'income' was mapped to 'fill', so each level of income was a separate group; since each of the bars is in a different group, they are dodged. With the geom_text, there was no grouping variable, and so all of the text at each x was in a single group. Since the text objects were all in one group, they should NOT have been dodged, but the dodging happened anyway. This is because the old code made some erroneous assumptions about the structure of the data.

To make it work now, you have to specify the grouping for the text, which can be done  with 'aes(group=income)'. (You could also use 'colour=income', but you probably don't want to change the text color.)

This code should do the trick:

library(ggplot2)

set.seed (66)
income <- rep(c("high","medium","low"), 5)
variable <- rep(c("USA","Switzerland","Spain","Greece","Japan"),3)
mean.value <- rnorm (15,5,2)
m.data <- data.frame (income,variable,mean.value)

pl  <- ggplot(data=m.data, aes(x=variable, y=mean.value, ymax=10))

pl  <- pl + geom_bar(aes(fill=income),position=position_dodge(0.9))
pl  <- pl + geom_text(aes(group=income, label=round(mean.value, 2)),
                      position=position_dodge(0.9), hjust=-0.5)

pl  <- pl + coord_flip()
pl

-Winston

messages.subject: Bug in facet_grid?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think I may have discovered a bug in facet_grid that is not present
in facet_wrap. If you look very carefully, there are differences
between the following two plots:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, carat)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_grid(.
~ cut)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, carat)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_wrap(~
cut, ncol=5)

Here is how I am looking at these:
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, carat)) + geom_boxplot() +
facet_grid(. ~ cut)
ggsave(p, file = "facet_grid.pdf")
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, carat)) + geom_boxplot() +
facet_wrap(~ cut, ncol=5)
ggsave(p, file = "facet_wrap.pdf")

A few of the medians are shifted, and some outliers differ. It also
seems like the drawing order differs (the "Very Good" label extends
outside the panel with facet_wrap, but not facet_grid).

I am using version 0.9.0 from CRAN, and here is my session info:

reshape2_1.2.1     scales_0.2.0       stringr_0.6
tools_2.14.2

I am working on a dataset where I think I am seeing a more extreme
version of this difference. Am I overlooking something, or could this
be a bug?

Right now, I am using facet_wrap as a workaround, since with my
dataset it produces a plot that looks identical to the standard
boxplot() function, and its medians look correct to me.

Cheers,
Ben

I think you want something like this,

geom_rect(aes(color=NULL, ymin=-1, ymax=1,xmin=0, xmax=200),
fill="red", alpha=0.5, data=data.frame(x=0,y=0))

without the dummy data, ggplot assumes that you're still using the
main data and overlays multiple rectangles (hence loses the
transparency). Not sure why inherit.aes doesn't appear to work here.

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Bug in facet_grid?
messages.body_plain:
On 3/12/2012 1:27 PM, Winston Chang wrote:
> I'm seeing this difference too. This seems odd. I've attached pictures of
> each, including an image showing the differences in red.
>
> The diff image was generated with 'compare' from ImageMagick:
>    compare facet-grid.png facet-wrap.png facet-diff.png
>
> -Winston

facet_grid is deleting duplicate data before the stats are run (I
think). Consider these much simpler examples:

DF <- expand.grid(alpha = letters[1:3],
                   beta = LETTERS[1:3])
DF <- cbind(DF, n = 1:27)

p <- ggplot(DF, aes(alpha, n)) + geom_boxplot()
pg <- p + facet_grid(.~beta)
pw <- p + facet_wrap(~beta, ncol=3)

DF2 <- DF[c(rep(1,10),2:27),]

p2 <- ggplot(DF2, aes(alpha, n)) + geom_boxplot()
p2g <- p2 + facet_grid(.~beta)
p2w <- p2 + facet_wrap(~beta, ncol=3)

pg and pw look the same; p2g looks like pg and pw; p2w does not. p2g
SHOULD look like p2w, not pg/pw.

I got a hint of what was happening by looking at the output of all.equal
on the results of ggplot_build on the original diamond plots; the
results of the stats were different, but what really tipped me off was
that the list of the outlier points were different lengths. However,
when looking at the points, some were listed multiple times (for wrap)
and there were no duplicates (grid).  From that I built this example
which shows the difference dramatically.

I've not looked at the code base to see where this is happening.

> SHOULD look like p2w, not pg/pw.

More evidence that it is in the facet and not something in boxplot:

ggplot(DF, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(aes(colour=beta),
fun.data="mean_cl_normal", position=position_dodge(width=0.2))
ggplot(DF2, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(aes(colour=beta),
fun.data="mean_cl_normal", position=position_dodge(width=0.2))
ggplot(DF, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal") +
facet_grid(.~beta)
ggplot(DF, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal") +
facet_wrap(~beta, ncol=3)
ggplot(DF2, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal") +
facet_grid(.~beta)
ggplot(DF2, aes(alpha, n)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal") +
facet_wrap(~beta, ncol=3)

those without, while facet_wrap with the duplicated data has the correct
summary (which agrees with what is drawn when differentiation is just by
colour and not facet).

Hi,

IIRC, this is relevant to previous discussion of removing duplicates
by facet_grid,
I cannot find pointer to it though...

Here is a workaround:

DF2 <- DF[c(rep(1,10),2:27),]

DF2$id <- 1:nrow(DF2)

p2 <- ggplot(DF2, aes(alpha, n)) + geom_boxplot()
p2g <- p2 + facet_grid(.~beta)
p2w <- p2 + facet_wrap(~beta, ncol=3)

messages.body_plain:
Another possibility is to plot the boxplot with hidden outlier points (using colour=NA), and then plot the outliers separately using geom_dotplot.

In the example below, I ripped out the code to do box plot calculations from stat_boxplot(), and simplified it. (Note that ggplot2's stat_boxplot does calculations slightly differently from the base graphics boxplot.) I think this does the right thing, but I can't guarantee that it works perfectly.

# This returns a data frame with the outliers only
find_outliers <- function(y, coef = 1.5) {
  qs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
  stats <- as.numeric(quantile(y, qs))
  iqr <- diff(stats[c(2, 4)])

  outliers <- y < (stats[2] - coef * iqr) | y > (stats[4] + coef * iqr)

  return(y[outliers])
}

library(MASS)  # Use the birthwt data set from MASS

# Find the outliers for each level of 'smoke'
library(plyr)
outlier_data <- ddply(birthwt, .(smoke), summarise, lwt = find_outliers(lwt))

# This draws an ordinary box plot
ggplot(birthwt, aes(x = factor(smoke), y = lwt)) + geom_boxplot()

# This draws the outliers using geom_dotplot
ggplot(birthwt, aes(x = factor(smoke), y = lwt)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = NA) +
  geom_dotplot(data = outlier_data, binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center",
               binwidth = 4)

You'll probably want to tweak 'binwidth' for your particular case.

Hope this helps! It's not a standard-looking boxplot, but it's probably less ugly than jittering the outliers.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
One more quick note. geom_dotplot draws circles with a fill and outline -- 'fill' and 'colour' respectively. When the points are this tiny, the outline can make them look like they're mushed together. You can remove the outline and make the dots look more distinct by setting 'colour=NA'.

ggplot(birthwt, aes(x = factor(smoke), y = lwt)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = NA) +
  geom_dotplot(data = outlier_data, binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center",

               binwidth = 4, colour = NA)

Bear in mind that on some platforms, the resulting circles might not be antialiased, and thus look jagged and asymmetrical.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Just to add a note to Josh's solution:

One of the differences in ggplot2-0.9.0 relative to 0.8.9 and earlier
is that other packages are no longer autoloaded with ggplot2; for
example, plyr and reshape are no longer 'co-loaded'. Moreover,
formatting and labeling functions that used to be in ggplot2-0.8.9
have been moved into the scales package along with a large number of
transformation functions, so if you intend to modify your positional
guides (axes) through transformation or axis label formatting, or
modify strip labels with a labeling function, you should load the
scales package along with ggplot2. It is probably not a bad idea to
write a custom .Rprofile function that loads a set of packages at
startup if you use them routinely in your work.

Dennis

On Tue, Mar 13, 2012 at 4:41 AM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just to add a note to Josh's solution:
>
> One of the differences in ggplot2-0.9.0 relative to 0.8.9 and earlier
> is that other packages are no longer autoloaded with ggplot2; for
> example, plyr and reshape are no longer 'co-loaded'. Moreover,
> formatting and labeling functions that used to be in ggplot2-0.8.9
> have been moved into the scales package along with a large number of
> transformation functions, so if you intend to modify your positional
> guides (axes) through transformation or axis label formatting, or
> modify strip labels with a labeling function, you should load the
> scales package along with ggplot2. It is probably not a bad idea to
> write a custom .Rprofile function that loads a set of packages at
> startup if you use them routinely in your work.

Good point.  Also, you may find the transition guide to 0.9
(spearheaded by Dennis) useful:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

many examples you find online (or in Hadley Wickham's ggplot2 book)
may not work exactly the same in 0.9.  The guide is helpful for
understanding how to adapt to the new, better world (better world of
software implementations of the grammar of graphics, that is).

messages.subject: Fractional numbers on y-axis in count-based barcharts
messages.subject_clean: Fractional numbers on y-axis in count-based barcharts
messages.body_plain:
When there are very few observations in each group, the axis labels for
bar charts are somewhat strange-looking, with decimal numbers (1.0)
instead of integers (1), along with fractional numbers (1.5). Example:

  x=c("A","B","B")
  qplot(x)

This shows a bar chart with axis breaks at 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0.

  qplot(rep(x,2))

This shows a bar chart with axis breaks at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Could it be changed so that bar charts (i.e., where y=..count..) would
always show integer labels on the y-axis?

In practice you wouldn’t normally plot data with so few oberservations,
but such data can easily occur when you use facetting on a large data
set (which was how I first observed this problem).

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer

messages.subject: Premium services
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm thinking about offering a membership service for ggplot2.
Everything that is currently available for free would keeping being
available for free: I'll still keep contributing to the mailing list
and the documentation will still be freely available, but I'd like to
introduce new services that would help raise money to develop ggplot2
and related packages. 100% of proceeds would go to funding activities
that would improve ggplot2 and related packages - none of it would go
to me.

I'd really appreciated your feedback through the brief survey
available at http://hadley.wufoo.com/forms/ggplot2-premium-services/ -
this will help me judge whether or not it's worthwhile to do.

Thanks!

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject: Remove gray gridlines
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 community,

I am producing a figure for publication and would like to remove the gray grid lines from the plot [these are present after using theme_bw()].  I have found numerous methods for doing this but they seem to not actually remove the grid lines or are broken/deprecated.

As version 0.9.0 has many new bells and whistles I figured I'd ask here to get the easiest way to approach the suppression of grid lines.  Here is my reproducible code:
library(ggplot2)
x <- ggplot(CO2, aes(x=uptake, group=Plant))
y <- x + geom_density(aes(colour=Plant)) + facet_grid(Type~Treatment)
y + theme_bw()

Here is a link to the example code in case the formatting of this email is messed up.
http://dl.dropbox.com/u/61803503/script.txt

Thank you in advance,
Tyler

messages.subject: Misaligned dotplot with dodging
messages.body_plain:
Running the following code leads to the dotplot elements being centered for the "H" factor as expected, but leads to dotplot elements of the "L" factor to be slightly offset to the left.

dat <- data.frame(letters=LETTERS[1:3], level = c("L","H"), size=rnorm(120))

ggplot(dat, aes(x=letters, y=size, fill = factor(level))) +
  geom_boxplot(position=position_dodge(width=1)) +
  geom_dotplot(position=position_dodge(width=1), binaxis="y", stackdir="center", binwidth=.1, alpha = .3)

Am I missing a parameter to adjust to center or is this a minor bug?

dotplot is a great feature that works perfectly without dodging as the following shows

ggplot(dat, aes(x=letters, y=size)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis="y", stackdir="center", binwidth=.1, alpha = .3)

Thanks for your help,

John

messages.subject: Factor ordering in facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 experts!

I am trying to plot some bar plot with errorbars ordered according to
two factors using "fill=factor_1" for factor_1 and facet_grid for
factor_2.

The problem that I have is that in the example below the ordering in
one cell of the facet_grid is according to the variable name on the x
axis. However I would like to order the bars according to factor_1 so
that bars of identical colors appear next to each other.

I am aware that I could change the ordering of the factor "name"
plotted on the x axis. However I have the same instances of the
variable "name" in the other cell of the facet grid and I would not
know how to give a different factor level to the same instance of a
variable?

Many thanks for your help & best wishes,
Jokel

Example code:

library(ggplot2)

# create some dummy data
name <- c("Name_1","Name_2","Name_3")
factor_1 <- c("A","B","A","B","A","B")
factor_2 <- c("C","C","C","D","D","D")
mean <- c(1.2,1.5,-2.1,1.9,-0.5,0.9)
sd <- c(0.2,0.5,0.1,0.1,0.25,0.4)
data <-
data.frame(name=name,factor_1=factor_1,factor_2=factor_2,mean=mean,sd=sd)

# plot
ggplot(data,aes(x=name, y=mean, fill=factor_1))
+geom_bar(stat="identity", positio="dodge")
+geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean-sd,ymax=mean+sd))+facet_grid(~factor_2,
scales="free_x", space="free")

x-axis ordered however you'd like. This is the solution I would use if
your x-axis ordering needs to change between panels. I can give you
sample code for this if useful.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Piggybacking on the sample code you've already given, I was thinking
about something like this, which produces a two-panel figure with
differently-ordered x axes.
Ben

# subset into two different data frames and relevel x axis factor
data1 <- subset( data, factor_2=="C" )
data1$name <- relevel( data1$name, "Name_3" )
data2 <- subset( data, factor_2=="D" )
data2$name <- relevel( data2$name, "Name_2" )

# two separate plots, one with no legend or y axis title
panela <- ggplot(data1,aes(x=name, y=mean, fill=factor_1))
+geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge")
+geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean-sd,ymax=mean+sd))+opts(legend.position =
"none")
panelb <- ggplot(data2,aes(x=name, y=mean, fill=factor_1))
+geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge")
+geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean-sd,ymax=mean+sd))
+opts(axis.title.y=theme_blank())

# draw 'em
grid.newpage()
pushViewport( viewport( layout=grid.layout( 1, 30 ) ) )
vplayout<-function( x, y ) viewport( layout.pos.row=x,

examples and using them for inspiration.

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

 I moved the alpha transparency snippet to geom_rect() rather than
inside scale_fill_manual() and that works:

#library('ggplot2')

(unemp <- qplot(date, unemploy, data=economics, geom="line",

                 xlab = "", ylab = "No. unemployed (1000s)"))

presidential <- presidential[-(1:3), ]

yrng <- range(economics$unemploy)
xrng <- range(economics$date)
unemp + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = start), data = presidential)
unemp + geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = start, xmax = end, fill = party),

                   ymin = yrng[1], ymax = yrng[2], alpha = 0.2,
                   data = presidential) +
         scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "red"))

Another option is to load the scales package first since the alpha()
function has been moved there; unfortunately, the transparency
rendered is 1 rather than the desired 0.2; try

library('scales')

unemp + geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = start, xmax = end, fill = party),

                   ymin = yrng[1], ymax = yrng[2],

                   data = presidential) +

         scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c("blue", "red"), 0.2))

I get the correct rectangles in red and blue, but they overwrite the
line plot in the region where the rectangles are defined with
transparency value 1. I don't know whether the problem is in
scale_fill_manual(), alpha() or their interaction, but it should be
looked at.

To me, the cleaner approach is to set alpha in geom_rect(); in
scale_fill_manual(), the code should work in principle, but I think
something is amiss at present. I'll raise an issue in the scales
package repo so that it will be in the pipeline for consideration.

Dennis

rescale) as its value, not a logical; that's the immediate source of
the error message. The next problem with your example is that the
object values is not defined, so if you take out the rescaler code,
another error message appears. However, if you take out both values =
and rescaler =, you will get a graphic; what do you want that's
different from

d + scale_colour_gradientn(colours = topo.colors(10))

?

messages.body_plain:

On Wed, Mar 14, 2012 at 12:10 PM, wong, honkit (Stephen)
<hon...@stanford.edu> wrote:
> Dear All,
> Let's say I have a following geom_point() plot, instead of labeling all the
> points using geom_text(),
> I only want to label a subset of points, how do I do that?

Define a subset data frame that contains the x and y coordinates
(possibly modified to correspond to the desired label locations) and
the text labels and use that as input to geom_text(). You also need to
remove the label = argument from the ggplot() call and leave it for
geom_text():

mtsub <- mtcars[sample(seq_len(nrow(mtcars)), 10), ]
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +
     geom_text(data = mtsub, aes(x = wt + 0.1, label =
rownames(mtsub)), hjust = 0, size = 4)

I just offset the x value by 0.1 and pushed the label to the right of
the point rather than in the center just for illustration.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: scale_y_log axis labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I would submit that your y-axis is misleading because it has equally
(linearly) spaced tick marks and nonlinear axis labels, and therefore
would likely confuse rather than edify a layperson. (I don't know many
non-mathematicians/scientists who can mentally interpolate values such
as 125 or 500 on such scales.) Here are a couple of ways to get what
you want, but I prefer the exponential labels because at least they
clarify that each break represents a power of 10. (BTW, this assumes
ggplot2-0.9.0 with the scales package loaded.)

library('ggplot2')
library('scales')

ggplot(junk, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
   scale_y_log10(breaks = trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x))

ggplot(junk, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
   scale_y_log10(breaks = trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x),
                         labels = trans_format("log10", math_format(10^.x)))

trans_breaks() and trans_format() are functions from the scales
package, as is math_format(). Functions that end in _breaks in the
scales package are meant to be used in conjunction with the breaks =
argument in a scale_*() function call, whereas functions that end in
_format are meant to be used with the labels = argument. The _format()
functions in the scales package replace and generalize the formatter =
argument in previous versions of ggplot2.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Bug in facet_grid?
messages.body_plain:
I think this problem is still present in the current version on github -- facet_grid is dropping duplicates. This illustrates it pretty clearly:

dat <- data.frame(x=rep(1:4, 10), g=rep(c("A","B"),each=20))
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x,x)) + geom_point(position="jitter")

# OK: 20 points in each facet
p + facet_wrap(~g)

# Not OK: 4 points in each facet
p + facet_grid(.~g)

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: scale_size errors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

In the new version of ggplot2 (0.9.0), many of the functions
pertaining to scales were rewritten and put into the scales package,
which is not autoloaded with ggplot2. The to = argument of
scale_size() in 0.8.9 has been changed to range = in the scales
package. So the short answer to your question is to use instead

p + scale_size(range=c(1,10))

If it doesn't work 'out of the box' with ggplot2-0.9.0, load the
scales package and try again. Your reproducible example worked for me
when I made the above change.

Dennis

On 2012-Mar-15, at 19:12 , evan l wrote:
>
> When I plot the data now using color = factor(out.class), each level is plotted independently (See image 1). This makes it impossible to see the original distribution. I'm looking for a solution to color/identify the outliers on one layer without splitting them up (see image 2 highlighted points).

>
> I could try to include the data, but I would have to change it to obfuscate it.

Indeed, when written this way the statistic (qq) is computed on the data split by factor level. You need to pre-compute your statistic manually and then plot it with geom_point(stat="identidy") (= geom_point()).

This should work:

	urdb.subset = urdb.subset[order(urdb.subset$SAMPLE)]
	urdb.subset$theoretical = qnorm(ppoints(nrow(urdb.subset))

	ggplot(urdb.subset) + geom_point(aes(x=theoretical, y=subet, colour=out.class))

messages.subject: ggmap v1.3 uploaded to cran
messages.body_plain:
New Features -
  1. a total overhaul of the geocode function (with backwards compatability).  geocode can now return more information such as the address (for when the location is lazy-specified, e.g. "the white house"), a bounding box, and political administrative bodies.
  2. revgeocode - a reverse geocoder using google maps.
  3. mapdist - a function to compute distances on maps using the google maps api.  distances in meters, km, and miles are returned as well as travel times in seconds, minutes and hours based on mode of transportation (driving, bicycling, or walking).  google query limit monitored with function distQueryCheck.
  4. route - a function to grab directions from google.  google query limit monitored with function routeQueryCheck. several options are available.
  5. qmap now accepts base_layer argument.
  6. geom_leg - geom_segment with rounded ends and made for the mercator projection.

Fixes -
  1. qmap and ggmapplot now deal properly with maprange.
 *2. the coordinate system is now properly set to a mercator projection.
  3. custom version of annotation_custom added (not exported) to allow for placement in and plotting of overlays with mercator projection.

New depends -
  1. rjson

A few screenshots attached from the examples.

Enjoy!

messages.subject: Gpplot2 feature request - no clipping
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

   When adding geom_text notation to a plot, the dimensions of the
text are not accounted for by the scaling mechanisms.  This can cause
clipping of text, deleting key information, such as labels.

   In base plot this can be avoided by changing the clipping rules for
the viewport - using par(xpd=NA).

   In ggplot, this option is not available, although the grid logic
allows it.

   I'd like to see an opt(xpd=NULL) or similar to allow clipping of
the plot areas to be disabled.

   This feature can also be used to create dramatic graphics where
points or bars extend out and over the titles.  To support this, we
should look to the new scale clipping features, plus a viewport
clipping rule.

-Alex

messages.subject_clean: removing the white space of panel margin
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Maybe you can take this and run with it to get what you want. Instead
of using a one-level factor that is more than capable of messing
things up, I used geom_segment() instead with a numeric x-axis. Here's
a reproducible example with fake data using ggplot2-0.9.0:

tst <- data.frame(idsort = round(runif(1000, 0, 2000), 0),
                    value = rnorm(1000, 0, 2))
ggplot(tst, aes(y = idsort, colour = value)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, yend = idsort)) +
    scale_colour_gradient2(expression(log2(Xrcc2mm/WT)), low="blue",

mid = "white", high="red",
             space = "Lab", midpoint = 0, breaks = c(-5,-2,0,2,5)) +

    opts(panel.background = theme_blank(), panel.border=theme_blank())

A couple of things you might try since you're using 0.9.0: (i) use
guide_legend() with the aes.override = argument to increase the
thickness of the lines in the legend (but not in the plot itself);
(ii) the x-labels are rather arbitrary and hence superfluous, so you
could get rid of them altogether.

Dennis

>      size=x,
>      fontsize=I(10),
>      linesize=4))

>
>   fixed:
>
>   qplot(data=X,fontsize=I(10),size=height,geom=c("text","point"))

Use ggplot() + geom_*** and you can easily achieve that:

ggplot(data=x) + geom_point(aes(size=x)) + geom_text(aes(), size=10, linesize=4)

everything you put inside aes is "mapped" to the data, everything outside aes is set as an absolute value.

messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Mar-16, at 07:20 , Alex@775 wrote:
>
>   stat_summary allows stats per x
>   stat_quantile allows stats per graph with some x correlation
>
>   I'd like to see a stat_group or similar that allows simple stat
> calculation per group.
>
>   ggplot() + stat_group(aes(group=cyl,x=mean(mpg),y=max(..y..)))

I thought this was already the case: if you use stat_summary and specify a colour or a group to aes, it should compute the summary per group (stat_qq does at least).

>   Alternativelty, I'd like to see function calculations in aes be
> applied per group:
>
>   for instance, I want to be able to plot a mean hline and vline on a
> scatter plot:
>
>> mc=mutate(mtcars,cyl=factor(cyl)
>
>> ggplot(data=mc,x=cyl,y=mpg) + geom_point() +
>> geom_hline(aes(y=mean(mpg),group=cyl))
>
>   another for instance, if I have grouped data, I might want to
> summarise and add a text label for each, in an appropriate location:
>
>> qplot(data=data.frame(x=rnorm(100),cat=sample(letters[1:4],
> 100,T)),
>     x=x)+geom_text(aes(group=cat,y=10,label=10,x=mean(x,y=max(x))))
>
>   Where x=mean is calculated per group.

The answer is probably: compute your summaries first and plot afterwards. plyr is there to help you compute such per-group summaries in one line. ggplot can't do everything.

> This does not currently
> operate like this.  It's odd that I can put a trendline or smoothed
> kernel line but not a mean line.

You can in those instances because the data is fed through a statistic which computes things per group (hence my remark above). In the syntax you present here, the data is fed to stat_identify which does not compute anything (and actually, the data fed to stat_identify is probably the result of the computation specified in the aes call already).

geoms.

This is perfect:

geoms:

Now the text is printed for EACH y, not for the summarised y.

If I could separate the aesthetics I would use

> qplot(data=mtcars, cyl, mpg, pointsize=5, fontsize=8, label=..y.., stat="summary", fun.y=mean, geom=c("point","text"))

or similar.

messages.subject: Re: hash of a ggplot object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christophe -

I think it's because there's a lot of stuff that happens (like setting up scales) when you print the ggplot object. Another way of forcing that all to happen is to use ggplot_build:

library("digest")
p<-ggplot(diamonds)+geom_point(aes(x=carat,y=price,colour=cut))
digest(p)

# "66ccf8e3a35e344f5af3d53434c71788"

invisible( ggplot_build(p) )  # There's a lot of output. Suppress it with invisible()
digest(p)
#"8486471ae63df5a97766e4acedc62ae8"

I don't know if these MD5 hashes are stable across platforms, though -- you'll notice that my numbers are different from yours, but that may be because I'm using a different version of ggplot2. The hashes will certainly change with different versions of ggplot2, because there are lots of internal changes.

I don't know the purpose of your tests, but I can tell you that I'm working on a visual testing system for ggplot2, so that it's possible to detect and visualize when changes to the code result in changes to the output. It's very much a work in progress, but it will hopefully be ready in the next week.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
I'm guessing it's got something to do with the random names assigned
to grobs. It would be nice if ggplot2 followed a naming scheme [*]
(also for post-processing, e.g interactive svg); I don't know if would
be easy to implement. A brute force approach would be to store
counters for each kind of grob, reinitialized for each new plot,

.rect <- 1
rectGrob <- function(..., name=NULL)
{
name <- if(is.null(name)) paste("rect.", .rect, sep="") else
                                       paste("name.", .rect, sep="")
.rect <<- .rect + 1
grid::rectGrob(..., name=name)
}

rectGrob()
rectGrob()

[*]: http://lattice.r-forge.r-project.org/Vignettes/src/naming-scheme/namingScheme.pdf

b.

messages.body_plain:
okay, stat_summary source was simple enough that I could puzzle it
out.

the stat reads the data object and consumes y (in the case of
stat_summary).

It generates data for one or more of fun.y, fun.ymax, fun.ymin

It generates a data frame with columns group, fun.y, fun.ymax,
fun.ymin (or some subset)

It snips off the fun. parts to leave just group, y, ymax, ymin.

These are then consumed by the geom.

I'm not sure whether the data output if available outside the 'layer'
or not.

Next - understanding layers.

On 2012-Mar-16, at 21:04 , Winston Chang wrote:
>
> I don't know the purpose of your tests, but I can tell you that I'm working on a visual testing system for ggplot2, so that it's possible to detect and visualize when changes to the code result in changes to the output. It's very much a work in progress, but it will hopefully be ready in the next week.

In the mean time and while a truly visual diff is being tested, a solution could be to save the plot to images and compare the images. In my case:

library("ggplot2")
p = qplot(1:10, 1:10)
ggsave("foo.png", p, width=5, height=5)

in two different R sessions gave me images with the same MD5:

MD5 (foo.png) = 7a2651157032ac1a34ef6140fae5f32e

messages.subject_clean: Passing a continuous fill variable to geom_dotplot
messages.body_plain:
I can't explain offhand the details of why it gives that error, but I can say that the way geom_dotplot is written, it _shouldn't_ work with a continuous fill.

It uses stat_bindot, which is similar to stat_bin -- essentially, it gets an input data frame, and then returns a data frame with an x value for each bin, and a count of the number of dots in the bin. The individual data points aren't in the new data frame; the new data frame only has counts. Then the geom_dotplot draws a stack of n dots for each bin. In other words, instead of "moving" the data points into each bin, it simply gets a count of the number of cases in each bin.

You get the same error if you try to use geom_histogram, which uses stat_bin.

d2 <- data.frame(v1 = runif(10, 1, 40),
                 v2 = runif(10, 0,1))

ggplot(d2, aes(x = v1, fill = v2)) + geom_dotplot()

# stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.
# Error in xyz %*% solve(M) : non-conformable arguments

ggplot(d2, aes(x = v1, fill = v2)) + geom_histogram()
# stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.
# Error in xyz %*% solve(M) : non-conformable arguments

-Winston

On 2012-Mar-16, at 18:22 , Alex@775 wrote:

> Now the text is printed for EACH y, not for the summarised y.
>
> If I could separate the aesthetics I would use
>
>> qplot(data=mtcars, cyl, mpg, pointsize=5, fontsize=8, label=..y.., stat="summary", fun.y=mean, geom=c("point","text"))
>
> or similar.

It seems you want:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=cyl, y=mpg)) +
	geom_point(stat="summary", fun.y=mean, size=5) +
	geom_text(stat="summary", fun.y=mean, mapping=aes(label=..y..), size=3, vjust=-1)

The stat argument is not inherited from the ggplot call to each layer (i.e. each geom) so you have to repeat it, and then you can customize the rest independently in each geom (while making sure that values that you want to *set*, rather than map, as the size here, are specified outside of the aes call.

messages.subject: Re: Passing a continuous fill variable to geom_dotplot
messages.subject_clean: Passing a continuous fill variable to geom_dotplot
messages.body_plain:
I'm glad you find it useful!
It occurred to me that it's possible to simulate what you're looking for if you're willing to have a discretized scale. (I think it's also perceptually easier to map colors back to numerical values using a discrete scale.) This requires a development branch of ggplot2 from github, where I added the ability to use stacking with dot plots.

library(devtools)
install_github('ggplot2', 'wch', 'dotplot-stack')
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(12)
d2 <- data.frame(v1 = runif(40, 1, 40),
                 v2 = runif(40, 0, 1))

# Convert the continuous values to discrete
d2$v3 <- cut(d2$v2, seq(0, 1, 0.2))

# Bin positions determined by data (dot-density)
ggplot(d2, aes(x = v1, fill = v3)) +
  geom_dotplot(stackgroups=TRUE, binpositions="all") +
  scale_fill_brewer()

# Regularly-spaced bins
ggplot(d2, aes(x = v1, fill = v3)) +
  geom_dotplot(stackgroups=TRUE, method="histodot") +
  scale_fill_brewer()

Make sure you have the latest devtools because there was a version that had problems installing branches from github.

I'm not sure if building in the capability to use a continuous fill would necessarily violate the grammar... I think it would require a complete reworking of the way stat_bindot works, and how geom_dotplot deals with the binned data. There's also the issue of how to vertically order the dots based on a continuous variable. I can't think of another case where something like this is done, so it would probably have to be a special case written into geom_dotplot. Overall, it probably makes more sense to just use the discrete method with stacking. Hopefully stacking will be in ggplot2 0.9.1.

-Winston

On Sat, Mar 17, 2012 at 1:47 PM, Tom W <thoma...@gmail.com> wrote:

> hi Winston--thanks for such an authoritative answer. I appreciate if there's a fundamental technical obstacle to implementing this option.
>
> I also think it would occasionally be useful to have this capability--I'm not sure that it would contradict the underlying grammar. But anyway, thanks so much for the work you've done implementing this new facility--the new features in 0.9 have been tremendous.
>
> Tom
>
>
> On Saturday, March 17, 2012 9:21:57 AM UTC-5, winston wrote:
> > I can't explain offhand the details of why it gives that error, but I can say that the way geom_dotplot is written, it _shouldn't_ work with a continuous fill.
> >
> > It uses stat_bindot, which is similar to stat_bin -- essentially, it gets an input data frame, and then returns a data frame with an x value for each bin, and a count of the number of dots in the bin. The individual data points aren't in the new data frame; the new data frame only has counts. Then the geom_dotplot draws a stack of n dots for each bin. In other words, instead of "moving" the data points into each bin, it simply gets a count of the number of cases in each bin.
> >
> > You get the same error if you try to use geom_histogram, which uses stat_bin.
> >
> > d2 <- data.frame(v1 = runif(10, 1, 40),
> >                  v2 = runif(10, 0,1))
> >
> > ggplot(d2, aes(x = v1, fill = v2)) + geom_dotplot()
> > # stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.
> > # Error in xyz %*% solve(M) : non-conformable arguments
> >

> > # stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.

messages.subject: Re: scale_fill_manual to create a custom legend : appears to do nothing.
messages.subject_clean: scale_fill_manual to create a custom legend : appears to do nothing.
messages.body_plain:
I have finally worked out how to use scale_colour_manual, scale_linetype_manual and scale_shape_manual. These can be used either separately or in combination. The linetype & shape are useful for black and white illustration. Further, if all three are used together then people who have trouble seeing the full range of rgb colours can interpret the graphs easily. I hope this example will help others.

To use the B&W version just delete or comment out the whole of the scale_colour_manual entry and remove "colour=variable" from aes(). Remember that each colour, linetype and shape manual function has to have a matching entry in aes(). No error is signalled if this is not done but the output will not be what you expect and the legends will probably not be correct.

You can miss out the facet_wrap as well but the graph will look odd because it has observations for three individuals.

How to use the shape (p196) , legends (p196) and colours (p102 on, p190) can be found in Hadley Wickham#s book "ggplot2". Details of how the palette of colours can be referenced is given in the example at the bottom of help page on palette {grDevices} in R on line documentation.

I am beholden to Dennis Murphy for his help with this. I hope this example will help others.

Ian.

### Data preparation

DSString <-
"NickN,       Weeks,  NoRiskM,  FunctM,   WellbeM
\"Runner\",   1,      2.1,      2.5,      1.3
\"Runner\",   2,      1.5,      1.7
\"Runner\",   3,      1.2,      1.5,
\"Jumper\",   1,      1.9,      2.4,      1.1
\"Jumper\",   2,      1.5,      1.2
\"Jumper\",   3,      1.2,      1.7,
\"Walker\",   1,      2.3,      2.9,      1.2
\"Walker\",   2,      1.2,      1.3
\"Walker\",   3,      1.2,      1.2,          "
DSString
DSTest <- read.csv( textConnection(DSString))
DSTest

library(reshape)
DSm <- melt(DSTest, id = c('Weeks','NickN'))

DSm
DSm$variable <- factor(DSm$variable, levels = c('NoRiskM', 'FunctM', 'WellbeM')) # set the levels so that the legend.type appear in the correct order
library(ggplot2)

#### plot with  linetype, shape & colout ################################

ggplot(DSm, aes(x = Weeks, y = value,

                colour = variable,          # delete if no matching scale_colour_manual
                linetype = variable,        # delete if no matching scale_linetype_manual
                shape = variable)) +       # delete if no matching scale_shape_manual
    geom_point() + geom_line(aes(group = variable)) +  ## you can set the point (shape) size & line thickness here.
    scale_colour_manual(breaks = levels(DSm$variable),
                        values = c('red', 'green', 'blue'),   ## you can get better palettes than this, but it works.

                        labels=c("No Risk", "Function", "Wellbeing"),
                        name="Means ") +

    scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(DSm$variable),
                        values = 1:3,   ## change these to get the linetype you want

                        labels=c("No Risk", "Function", "Wellbeing"),
                        name="Means ") +

    scale_shape_manual(breaks = levels(DSm$variable),
                        values = 1:3,   ## change these to get the shapes you want

                        labels=c("No Risk", "Function", "Wellbeing"),
                        name="Means ") +
    opts( title="Means by Week by Nick Name" ) +
    scale_x_continuous("Week Number", limits = c(0, 5)) + ##set horiz scale x
    scale_y_continuous("Mean Score", limits = c(0, 3)) +  ##sets vert scale y
    facet_wrap(~NickN, ncol=3, drop=F) ## for each NickN, 3 cols, drop=F: do not drop missing

messages.subject: Multiple time-series using qplot
messages.body_snippet:
Is it possible or even sensible to use qplot for multiple time-series?

I have 3 series that I want to plot against time. Note that the series are over-lapping in time but some are longer than others.

messages.subject: Re: Multiple time-series using qplot
messages.body_plain:
Keith,

you can use qplot for showing multiple time series - the easiest way would be to melt the variables into a single variable and then plot:

X1 <- rnorm(100)
X2 <- rnorm(mean=3, 100)
X3 <- rnorm(mean=1, 100)
frame <- data.frame(X1=X1, X2=X2, X3=X3)

library(ggplot2)
frame$id <- 1:nrow(frame)
framem <- melt(frame, measure.vars=1:3)
qplot(id, value, group=variable, geom="line", colour=variable, data=framem)

Heike

>From your write up, I conclude that ggplot2 membership and premium support should be two separate things:

- the membership could resemble that of many other scientific societies:
	. a yearly fee of $20-30, which people pay to signify their interest in the subject, to support ggplot. If you can reward donators with cheap/free memorabilia, that's even better. Ideas: a t-shirt, a mug, an acknowledgment on the website (for those who want it), the right to add "I am a ggplot supporter" message in their email signature, a badge on their website, a newsletter that you (and/or others) would edit with "the best of ggplot on the web" etc.
	. additional fees for more expensive goods, such as a (signed) copy of the book (in other societies, this is typically journal subscriptions)

- the premium support system could be on a subscription or time-billing basis and would work as any other consultancy work would.
You would have to figure out a good business strategy to make this work of course, but something based on increasingly expensive plans such as :
	. free : the ggplot mailing list !
	. 50$ a year : 15 premium-support emails
	. 100$ a year : 30 premium-support emails or skype calls, discount on 1 online course
	etc.
is common with web services and easily grasped by most people.

I think these two items should be kept separate because they target different people and would be paid with different sources of money. The membership would probably interest most people on this mailing list and would be paid with personal money. The premium support targets very specific needs (some of which you highlight in the document you sent) and would probably be paid with company money.

That's just the opinion of a future ggplot membership subscriber of course ;)

On 2012-Mar-17, at 17:46 , Alex@775 wrote:
>
> Yes, Thats the fall back solution, but writing code twice creates the
> potential for bugs.
>
> In principle, does the multiple aes with overriding seem unreasonable?
>
> I can work up a patch.
>
> Should this convo really be in Dev?  I'm not an existing contributor
> to ggplot2.

Yes you might want to move this to ggplot-dev.

Ultimately it's for Hadley to decide but I would guess the change needed to get this working in a general manner is not trivial.

In addition, from a user perspective, it complicates the interface to have several names for the same aesthetic (size and pointsize for point, size and textsize for text etc.).
Furthermore, still from a UX perspective, I always thought that the "true" ggplot syntax is the ggplot + geom one. qplot is just a shorthand, for quick jobs and/or to make users of the base plot somewhat at home. So you can't ask qplot to do everything that ggplot + geom does, otherwise, it would become too complicated and defeat its purpose of being a quick, simple shorthand.

But again, that's only my point of view and only Hadley can really say what he wants qplot to be.

Use

or

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 docs sneak peek
messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Mar-17, at 16:08 , Hadley Wickham wrote:
>
> Over the last couple of days, I've been hard at work preparing a
> replacement for the outdated ggplot2 documentation website:
> http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/docs/.  It's not 100% done, but it's getting
> pretty close, and it's probably at a useful point for feedback.
>
> The cool thing about the website is that it's generated from the
> package documentation so it will always be perfectly in sync.  The
> same code (https://github.com/hadley/staticdocs) can be used for any
> package, so I'll hopefully be able to get plyr and reshape2 docs up on
> their respective websites too.

It's great that it will be kept up to date, the abundance of links and the clean layout are really appreciable. But I am afraid it lost the main appeal of the old site: the visual index. The small thumbnails allowed to quickly browse the various functions and get a feel for their use. It was great to discover geoms or to guess which scale function one should use. It gave a real incentive to go read the help on the website rather than in R's help browser.

With the new site, I'm not sure the incentive would be as strong. The fact that every function name is a link is nice, but with the new ggplot help, most functions that really deserve a link are already linked in the "See also" part. The graphical output after each example is of course very nice, but I think it can also be available in R's built in html help (I use inline text-based help in a terminal but I have seen people with graphs in their help files in previous versions of ggplot at least) and example() is not very hard to run. On the other hand, going to the site has a cost: having a web browser open instead of the clean help panel of RStudio for example, send to an external website for non-ggplot2 functions, without the usual navigation of the regular help browser, etc.

Also, compared to the old site, I am missing the list of accessible aesthetics for each geom, and in particular the required vs facultative ones.

Finally, and that's more a general remark about ggplot's help, I find that having a mix of true functions (such as aes, aes_string) and "fake" ones which are only used to document usage (such as aes_group_order or aes_colour_fill_alpha) is confusing, especially given the similarity of names. Another good (bad?) example is alpha, which is a function that was in ggplot, is now in scale, but which now also has a help page in ggplot. It's not the documenting the alpha() function anymore, just the usage of the alpha aesthetic, but someone looking for the function might not understand why it is not available. Maybe prefix all those "fake" functions with doc_ or usage_? In any case, the website could be a great opportunity to differentiate the true functions from the others, and appropriately show the relevant "usage" documentation when browsing a particular function (show links or even inline versions of all the aes_*** usage help files when reading the help of aes).

Thanks for all your efforts. I don't want to sound too harsh even though I probably do :-/ . I really think that the thumbnails provided large additional value to the website.

Jean-Olivier Irisson

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have some reservations on the premium support idea.

It may be that the way ggplot2's help and development work now --
organically driven by enthusiasts from this list, R-help, SO, github
-- are already close to optimal (a trade-off between how many hours
dedicated but busy people are willing to spend on it, and the quality
of the contributions).
Charging for some select answers would certainly alter that delicate
balance. For one thing, if one pays for an answer, one should expect
an authoritative one. But these can often only come from a handful of
people, and their professional consulting rate would be very high as
you point out.

I don't know what motivates us folks to answer currently; it's
probably a variable mix of reasons, from improving your online
reputation, learning, entertainment, killing time, showing off,
curiosity, urge to teach things, genuine help, etc. It could be argued
that raising money would never work as well as an incentive, and could
also have detrimental effects on the personal drive of some list
members.

Are there examples of open-source communities that have set up a
successful premium membership? Maybe we can learn from their story.

If money can speed up the development of ggplot2, I think the other
options (t-shirts, books, donations) are much less interfering; in
this regard would it not be an option to simply add a line to the
ggplot2 mailing list signature saying that donations are welcome?

Just my 2 cents

Cheers,

baptiste

> curiosity, urge to teach things, genuine help, etc. It could be argued
> that raising money would never work as well as an incentive, and could
> also have detrimental effects on the personal drive of some list
> members.

I agree that the paid support could discourage those who basically do it for free right now. I personally consider the time spend answering questions as a way to "pay" for this otherwise free bounty that is ggplot (and I don't do it as often as I should given this standard) but it's difficult to know the motivation of everyone indeed.

> Are there examples of open-source communities that have set up a
> successful premium membership? Maybe we can learn from their story.

Ubuntu and Canonical spring to mind, but the size of the communities are not the same. In addition, I think that most canonical employees are not involved in the Ubuntu support forums, so there is already a clear separation between the free, user-powered support and the paid one. This wasn't true for ggplot (and I would bet that a great part of its initial momentum came from the excellent support of Hadley on the mailing lists).

I can't find another example.

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
messages.body_plain:
On 03/20/2012 05:10 AM, Jean-Olivier Irisson wrote:

>  I agree that the paid support could discourage those who basically
> do it for free right now. I personally consider the time spend
> answering questions as a way to "pay" for this otherwise free bounty
> that is ggplot (and I don't do it as often as I should given this
> standard) but it's difficult to know the motivation of everyone
> indeed.

There's significant research on this topic.  I recommend 'Predictably
Irrational', by Dan Ariely, as a readable sketch, aimed at the general
public but reasonably detailed.

The bit most relevant to this conversation is "The Cost of Social
Norms -- Why we are happy to do things, but not when we are paid to do
them."  The key points might be phrased something like this:

+ It's easy to move an individual from viewing behavior as "social" to
   seeing it as participation in a "market".

+ It's difficult to move the other way, from market-encourage behavior
   to socially-encouraged; it's also difficult to maintain both
   motivations simultaneously.

+ Market behavior outcompetes social behavior in a community.

To quote:

"When a social norm collides with a market norm, the social norm goes
away for a long time.  In other words, social relationships are not
easy to reestablish. Once a social norm is trumped by a market norm,
it will rarely return."

I'm not (quite) speaking against paid support; I'm more pointing out
the mental pitfalls to which people are heir, once they start
accepting pay for behavior they were once proud to do for free as a
social duty.

Hadley's manner towards his community is IMO nearly a textbook for
managing such behavior; he pushes credit out to the community.  Other
humans who hope to get some regular market reinforcement from ggplot2
ought to follow his example and keep an eye on their attitudes; The
market tendencies are written deep in our genes in many ways.

- Allen S. Rout

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 docs sneak peek
messages.body_plain:
On 17 Mar 2012, at 3:08 PM, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> Over the last couple of days, I've been hard at work preparing a
> replacement for the outdated ggplot2 documentation website:
> http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/docs/.  It's not 100% done, but it's getting
> pretty close, and it's probably at a useful point for feedback.

Hi hadley,
So, first off: Thanks for working hard on this.

> The cool thing about the website is that it's generated from the
> package documentation so it will always be perfectly in sync.

I think in R, because people are busy, and no-one’s paid, there’s a perfectly reasonably desire to keep things simple and automated. If that’s the goal then this hits it.

However, Just as R package “documentation” files, with their alphabetical listings of everything, (even data files!!) mixed up with internal helpers and key functions buried amongst that are almost no use to someone looking for help.

Automated documentation, built out of the code and it’s parameters, is that it really leaves a lot to be desired for someone with a question in their mind (and that’s about everyone).

What works really well is curated task-driven pages with clear explanatory text, well-chosen (and commented) examples, and a well organized contents page

My positive suggestions would be

Try and add hints to the list generator so that, for instance, it can collect example data files together under a “Data files” heading.
Even a set of basic heading hints, embedded in the source that this program could use to aggregate:
# Core functions
# Example Data
# Sub functions
  ## Aesthetics
  ## Geoms
 ...

Try to prioritize the tiny set of commonly used functions over all the others. Create a learning curve.

Give examples, with comments as to what the example is trying to do, all the parameters named, links to the graphical output...
Like the old diamonds book…

Link everything: Make it possible to get from qplot to other pages that use it, or expand on it, or supplant it, or give examples for it…
Link to stack overflow, and crossvalidated, and to bloggers who’ve used the package and tried to give good specific examples.
Have a search box which aggregates stackoverflow, r-help with tags for ggplot2…

Negative comments
This alphabetical list of  250+ functions will not help people trying to learn ggplot or solve a problem
Probably doesn’t need to have a dedicate dbox of dependencies, etc. Maybe this whole page could be an appendix: an alphabetical listing and technical data?
The top link of "ggplot2-package: ggplot2” takes you to this:

I think at that point most people will give up (some will cry :-) )

Take this with a grain of salt, I’ve just been teaching  in R with bright post-graduates highlights and it drives home repeatedly to me how they see R as almost purposively obscure and inconsistent during their learning (despite their also loving how R gets things done when it does work smoothly for them)

There’s also a _very_ low bar set for help R in general, with error messages that help you solve the error frowned upon.

Compare to a well organized and helpful site, like  http://www.statmethods.net

I think he went backwards with the reworking, but it is still a great place to learn R from.

My guess is that if you stick a markdown wiki into had.co.nz <http://had.co.nz>, then users can take care of all of this for you: many of us like to store knowledge publicly.

best, t

>>
>>> In addition, from a user perspective, it complicates the interface to have several names for the same aesthetic (size and pointsize for point, size and textsize for text etc.).
>>
>> I would argue quite strongly that they are NOT the same aesthetic at all, in fact I'd prefer if there was no common name.  However, that would break backward compatibility.
>
> I think of them as properties, which have a different aesthetic consequence depending on the object. It' s important to have consistent names to make them discoverable.
>
> In addition, if you go that route, the size if points is actually diameter so that would be a better name. But diameter is probably more difficult to understand for other shapes, so it becomes hard to find a good name for it that isn't size.
>
>>> Furthermore, still from a UX perspective, I always thought that the "true" ggplot syntax is the ggplot + geom one. qplot is just a shorthand, for quick jobs and/or to make users of the base plot somewhat at home. So you can't ask qplot to do everything that ggplot + geom does, otherwise, it would become too complicated and defeat its purpose of being a quick, simple shorthand.
>>
>> I was only using qplot for compactness.
>
> OK
>
>> However, you should note that the stat_ methods, and the layer method accept multiple geoms.
>
> I know but that supposes that the aesthetic mapping is the same for all geoms, which is probably true in many cases. If you want to do something different in each layer, then it seems conceptually fitting to have to specify each layer separately.
>
>>> But again, that's only my point of view and only Hadley can really say what he wants qplot to be.
>>
>> And a valid one.  I use ggplot a lot, and I love it, and want to make it easier for new users and maintainers to understand and use it.  As part of this I want to file off the sharp edges that have hit me and every new user.  The aesthetic issue is only one of them (and probably quite private to me).
>
> That's the best reason to provide feedback and I saw you provided a lot of it, which is good.
>
> For this particular issue, I think the documentation of ggplot is misleading in that it presents qplot quite often and uses several different plot constructions, giving the impression that all constructions are equally powerful. Hadley agreed that the examples should be made more consistent (and I am working on it when I can). The idea is to start the documentation of all functions with the more versatile syntax:
>
> 	ggplot() + geom_***(mapping=aes(whatever), data=mydata) + geom_***(…
>
> i.e. specify each layer completely and independently from the others. Then, in later examples, we would start to introduce shorthands such as:
> - specify stuff in the ggplot call which gets inherited by all layers
> - save the plot to an object and modify the object
> - use qplot
> etc.
> But these constructions are special cases of the general syntax, faster to write but less powerful. The verbosity of the general syntax makes it completely clear.
>
> Jean-Olivier Irisson

Folks,
 The following function works if I repeat each statement on the
command line.

I successfully create an "inset" graph within a graph using the
viewport commands and following the example of the ggplot2 book
section 8.4.2

When I call it as a function I only get the inset graph. I am sure
that there must be something that I am missing regarding the way pdf()
or par() works in a function.

Thanks for your time,
KW

Here is my code:

pAndLgraph<-function(cf.data, upFront) {
  # Create p and l in millions
  pl<-pAndL(cf.data, upFront)/1000
  names(pl)<-c("P.And.L")
  # This is all the p and l less than the maximum value. I.e. the tail
  pl.tail<-as.data.frame(pl[var1.pl <http://var1.pl><max(var1.pl <http://var1.pl>)])
  names(pl.tail)<-c("P.And.L")

  pl.plot<-qplot(P.And.L, data = pl, geom = "density", size = I(.75))
  pl.tail.plot<-qplot(P.And.L, data = pl.tail, geom = "density")
  pl.tail.plot<-pl.tail.plot + theme_gray(9) + labs(x = NULL, y =
NULL) +
    opts(plot.margin = unit(rep(0,4), "lines"))

  pdf(file.choose(), width = 4, height = 4)
  vp2<-viewport(width = .4, height = .4, x = .3, y = .7)
  pl.plot
  print(pl.tail.plot, vp = vp2)
  dev.off()
}

On 21 March 2012 08:26, Brandon Hurr <brando...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just out of curiosity, why is that the case?

ggplot2 and lattice produce plots using grid graphics, where one can
separate the production of grobs (GRaphical OBjects) that can be
stored as a description of the plot, and the actual drawing where
these grobs are pushed onto the device. With raw grid objects this is
the distinction between,

g = grid::rectGrob() # create a rectangle, draw nothing
grid::grid.draw(g) # draw it

ggplot2 and lattice work at a higher level, and define a print()
method to display the graphics description containing many grobs and
viewports. In the interactive read-eval-print R session, objects are
printed when their name is invoked on the command line. This is not
the case within a function, or in non-interactive mode, hence the need
to explicitely call print().

HTH,

b.

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm trying to facet a bunch of dotplots along with their lm fits.
Currently, I loop over the various subsets of the data to create a list
of lm fits.  I can facet the dot plots, but I'm not sure how to get the
fits from from the list of lm-objects in there.

pseudo-code:
    fit_list = list()
    for (i in species) {
        sub_data = subset(alldata, species == i)
        fit_list[i] = lm(growth ~ size, data=sub_data)
    }

    ggplot(data = alldata, aes(x=size, y=growth)) + geom_point() +
        facet_wrap(~ species)

The above gets me the faceted dot plots.  I don't think geom_smooth
handles lists of lm fits.  Any suggestions are greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Allie

messages.subject: Re: faceting multiple lm models
messages.body_plain:
If I understand you right, you want the fit line for each facet to
depend only on the points of that facet: I think what you are looking
for is

ggplot(alldata, aes(x = size, y = growth)) + geom_point() +
stat_smooth(method = "lm") + facet_wrap( ~ species)

E.g.,

data(diamonds)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) + geom_point() +
stat_smooth(method = "lm") +  facet_wrap(~ cut, ncol = 1)

Note that in each facet, the resulting line is different.

Hope this helps,
Michael

On 3/20/2012 10:40 AM, Timothy Bates wrote:
> On 17 Mar 2012, at 3:08 PM, Hadley

> Wickham<hadley-OhmvVRJSr/I...@public.gmane.org>  wrote:
>> Over the last couple of days, I've been hard at work preparing a
>> replacement for the outdated ggplot2 documentation website:
>> http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/docs/.  It's not 100% done, but it's
>> getting pretty close, and it's probably at a useful point for
>> feedback.
>
> Hi hadley, So, first off: Thanks for working hard on this.
>
>
>> The cool thing about the website is that it's generated from the
>> package documentation so it will always be perfectly in sync.
>

> I think in R, because people are busy, and no-oneï¿½s paid, thereï¿½s a

> perfectly reasonably desire to keep things simple and automated. If

> thatï¿½s the goal then this hits it.
>
> However, Just as R package ï¿½documentationï¿½ files, with their

> alphabetical listings of everything, (even data files!!) mixed up
> with internal helpers and key functions buried amongst that are
> almost no use to someone looking for help.
>

> Automated documentation, built out of the code and itï¿½s parameters,

> is that it really leaves a lot to be desired for someone with a

> question in their mind (and thatï¿½s about everyone).

>
> What works really well is curated task-driven pages with clear
> explanatory text, well-chosen (and commented) examples, and a well
> organized contents page

In principle, I think you are right. However, the problem is that
carefully curated information can never really keep up with
automatically organized data. The problems with volume and immediacy are
too great. Compare, for example, DMOZ vs Google (or a more fair
comparison may be Wikipedia vs Google).

The place where this works well is books, because the expected updating
cycle (new editions) are much longer and level of being out of date is
accepted. Not to mention a different economic model.

> My positive suggestions would be
>
> Try and add hints to the list generator so that, for instance, it can

> collect example data files together under a ï¿½Data filesï¿½ heading.

> Even a set of basic heading hints, embedded in the source that this
> program could use to aggregate: # Core functions # Example Data # Sub
> functions ## Aesthetics ## Geoms ...

Some of this is doable automatically. Breaking out datasets is the
easiest. They are (should be) tagged with the keyword datasets.
Unfortunately, the list of allowable keywords is fixed, and looking over
them (gtools::keywords()) doesn't necessarily give a good set of generic
ones for this purpose. One that I was looking for in particular is
something that would tag a page as general descriptive documentation and
not documenting a specific function. "documentation" is more about
functions which are designed to manage, manipulate, and display
documentation. Maybe it should all go together as part of "package" (but
I think that is abusing that). There needs to be a "concepts" or
something like that. (The counter argument being that that kind of
documentation belongs in a vignette, not Rd files.)

The other facility available is the @family tag of roxygen, and the see
also section of the Rd files in general. Unfortunately, the @family tag
does not survive to the Rd files; at that point it is just a list of
linked functions.

I decided to try and see what could be pulled out in terms of automated
cluster detection of Rd files based on cross references.

library("tools")
library("plyr")
library("igraph")

tagsets <- function(l, tags) {
     has_tag <- ((attr(l, "Rd_tag") == tags[1]) & is.null(attr(l,
"Rd_option"))) #Rd_option indicates other package
     if (is.recursive(l)) {
         tags <- tags[c(!has_tag, rep(TRUE, length(tags)-1))]
         llply(l, tagsets, tags)
     } else {
         if(has_tag) {
             l
         }
     }
}

Rdfiles <- list.files("ggplot2/man", pattern="Rd", full.names=TRUE)
seealso <- ldply(Rdfiles, function(Rdfile) {
     Rd <- parse_Rd(Rdfile)
     fun.name <http://fun.name> <- unlist(tagsets(Rd, c("\\name", "VERB")))
     alias.names <- unlist(tagsets(Rd, c("\\alias", "VERB")))
     alias.names <- setdiff(alias.names, fun.name <http://fun.name>)
     seealsos <- unlist(tagsets(Rd, c("\\seealso", "\\link", "TEXT")))
     if (length(seealsos) > 0 | length(alias.names) > 0) {
         rbind(
               data.frame(fun=fun.name <http://fun.name>, seealso=c(seealsos, alias.names)),
               ldply(alias.names, function(alias) {
                   data.frame(fun=alias, seealso=c(fun.name <http://fun.name>,
setdiff(alias.names, alias), seealsos))
               }))
     } else {
         NULL
     }})

g <- graph.data.frame(seealso, directed=TRUE)

g.cl <http://g.cl> <- maximal.cliques(g)
llply(g.cl <http://g.cl>[sapply(g.cl <http://g.cl>, function(cl) {length(cl)>3})], function(cl)
{V(g)[cl]})

This identifies the clusters:

[1] "geom_abline"  "geom_hline"   "geom_segment" "geom_vline"

[[2]]

[1] "guide_colourbar" "guide_colorbar"  "guide_legend"    "guides"

[[3]]

[1] "hmisc"          "mean_cl_boot"   "mean_cl_normal" "mean_sdl"
[5] "median_hilow"

[1] "position_dodge"    "position_fill"     "position_identity"
[4] "position_jitter"   "position_stack"

  [1] "scale_colour_brewer"     "scale_color_brewer"

adjustments (5th one), position scales (9th one), guides (2nd one), and
colour scales (6th one). Coming up with automatic names to categorize
these may not be easy, though.

> Try to prioritize the tiny set of commonly used functions over all
> the others. Create a learning curve.

This gets into the realm of territory of the difference between a
tutorial and a reference manual. A tutorial is designed to show how
something is to be used: the various ways to approach it and the idioms
of it. This is better as a vignette (or book). A reference manual is to
list the gritty details. It should be organized as well as possible, but
it serves a different purpose. Rd files are reference manuals.

> Give examples, with comments as to what the example is trying to do,
> all the parameters named, links to the graphical output... Like the

> old diamonds bookï¿½

>
> Link everything: Make it possible to get from qplot to other pages
> that use it, or expand on it, or supplant it, or give examples for

> itï¿½

This is an interesting idea. Using a parser on the examples, it should
be possible to find every place a specific function is used. Maybe the
package that marks up the code can also include unique anchor links for
each line which can be linked to on a separate page, or in a section at
the bottom (examples of this/these functions on other pages). Extracting
appropriate context would not be easy, so maybe just a static line above
and below that with a link to the exact spot that function is used on
another page.

> Link to stack overflow, and crossvalidated, and to bloggers

> whoï¿½ve used the package and tried to give good specific examples.

> Have a search box which aggregates stackoverflow, r-help with tags

> for ggplot2ï¿½

Here, I'm not in agreement with you. This documentation, whatever it is,
should be self contained. Not that those are not good resources (and
maybe a single spot which lists other resources in general is itself a
fine thing).

> Negative comments This alphabetical list of  250+ functions will not
> help people trying to learn ggplot or solve a problem Probably

> doesnï¿½t need to have a dedicate dbox of dependencies, etc. Maybe this

> whole page could be an appendix: an alphabetical listing and

> technical data? The top link of "ggplot2-package: ggplot2ï¿½ takes you
> to this:

>
>
>
>
>
>
> I think at that point most people will give up (some will cry :-) )

I almost did ;)

But I would still argue that "learn ggplot" is the realm of a
tutorial/vignette/book, not the manual pages.

> Take this with a grain of salt, Iï¿½ve just been teaching  in R with

> bright post-graduates highlights and it drives home repeatedly to me
> how they see R as almost purposively obscure and inconsistent during
> their learning (despite their also loving how R gets things done when
> it does work smoothly for them)
>

> Thereï¿½s also a _very_ low bar set for help R in general, with error

> messages that help you solve the error frowned upon.

I don't think they are frowned on so much as no one wants to put in the
effort to do better. They'd rather work on something else.

> Compare to a well organized and helpful site, like
> http://www.statmethods.net
>
> I think he went backwards with the reworking, but it is still a great
> place to learn R from.
>
> My guess is that if you stick a markdown wiki into had.co.nz <http://had.co.nz>, then
> users can take care of all of this for you: many of us like to store
> knowledge publicly.

There is the Wiki on the GitHub site:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki
It's got some good resources in it, and it is publicly editable (well,
with a github login).

My question is what is the best way to create graphics to be inserted into the report? Do I create them full size and then shrink them after I import them into the document? Should I create them as PDF or jpg or png?

For example I tried to use pdf("file.name <http://file.name>", width = 3, height = 3) with a graph I had already programmed. I'm sure you can guess what the result was: the graph was full size but squished in a tiny space.

I know these are general questions but I am sure some of you have come upon and solved these issues in your own work.

Thanks so much for your time,
KW

messages.body_plain:
Create the graphs as PNG files and insert into the document. ggsave is very easy and robust to use for this, or RStudio makes it painfully simple to save graphs as well.

There's nothing per se wrong with saving as a PNG file and then making the graph smaller (proportionally), but it can make the graph unreadable. Axes labels in particular are liable to become difficult to read and the mixed sizes will screw with the polished look of your report.

If you want to edit / annotate the graphs you can save as PDF and then edit in e.g. Illustrator.

Also, don't use png(); use ggsave, e.g.

ggsave(filename="mygraph.png",plot=plot)

Full syntax is

ggsave(filename=default_name(plot), plot = last_plot(), device=default_device(filename), path = NULL, scale=1, width=par("din")[1], height=par("din")[2], dpi=300, keep = plot$options$keep, drop = plot$options$drop, ...)

> There's nothing per se wrong with saving as a PNG file and then making the graph smaller (proportionally), but it can make the graph unreadable. Axes labels in particular are liable to become difficult to read and the mixed sizes will screw with the polished look of your report.
>
> If you want to edit / annotate the graphs you can save as PDF and then edit in e.g. Illustrator.
>
> Also, don't use png(); use ggsave, e.g.
>
> ggsave(filename="mygraph.png",plot=plot)
>
> Full syntax is
>
> ggsave(filename=default_name(plot), plot = last_plot(), device=default_device(filename), path = NULL, scale=1, width=par("din")[1], height=par("din")[2], dpi=300, keep = plot$options$keep, drop = plot$options$drop, ...)
>
