messages.subject: Re: Best practice
messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Mar-21, at 14:04 , Keith Weintraub wrote:
>
> I have one plot that uses viewports. Does ggsave "play nice" with that?

It should.

Regarding the resolution, about which you asked earlier, it all depends on how the document will be used. Journals often require a resolution for raster images (most of the time 600dpi). For printing on a regular printer, 300dpi is usually fine. To view the document on screen only, 150dpi should be enough.

Overall, the strategy to adopt unfortunately depends on many factors (which software is used, on what platform, what is the purpose of the document, what are the quality requirements). My general advice would be:

- if it is for a quick job, with no particular requirements, use 150 dpi PNGs at the final size they should have on the document; they will be compatible with everything and shouldn't weight too much

- if you want quality, create PDFs and insert them in the final layout in Pages only (Word on windows does not play nice). I would also create them at 1.5 or 2 times the final size and increase the font size to compensate for the later shrinking; this makes the lines (in particular grid lines) thiner and usually looks better in a high quality document. You could also alter the theme to make grid lines and other elements thinner. Of course, this might juste be a matter of personal preference ;)

Jean-Olivier Irisson

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 docs sneak peek
messages.body_plain:
> So, first off: Thanks for working hard on this.

You're welcome.

> However, Just as R package “documentation” files, with their alphabetical
> listings of everything, (even data files!!) mixed up with internal helpers
> and key functions buried amongst that are almost no use to someone looking
> for help.

I partially agree.  There are two types of people looking for help:
people who know what they want to do, they just needed some help on
how to do it; and people who are struggling to define the problem they
are trying to solve. Documentation helps the former, but not the
latter.

> Automated documentation, built out of the code and it’s parameters, is
> that it really leaves a lot to be desired for someone with a question in
> their mind (and that’s about everyone).
>
> What works really well is curated task-driven pages with clear explanatory
> text, well-chosen (and commented) examples, and a well organized contents
> page

Yes, I totally agree.  However, the fact of the matter is that I don't
have time to write these, and no one else has yet stepped up to the
plate.  The point of the new documentation system is to reduce the
amount of work to update the website, and in the longer term tie in to
a better workflow for improving the documentation.  By the end of the
summer, I hope to have an in depth tutorial written on how to
contribute, and each documentation page will link back to the original
source on github so people can relatively easily contribute
improvements.

> My positive suggestions would be
>
> Try and add hints to the list generator so that, for instance, it can
> collect example data files together under a “Data files” heading.
> Even a set of basic heading hints, embedded in the source that this
> program could use to aggregate:
> # Core functions
> # Example Data
> # Sub functions
>   ## Aesthetics
>   ## Geoms
>  ...

This is something I will do.

> Try to prioritize the tiny set of commonly used functions over all the
> others. Create a learning curve.

This, I think, is the job of the book, not the documentation.

> Give examples, with comments as to what the example is trying to do,
> all the parameters named, links to the graphical output...
> Like the old diamonds book…

There are about 1,200 examples in the documentation - it's simply too
much work to describe every one extensively.  My expectation is not
that people will be able to learn ggplot2 from scratch from the
documentation, but the documentation should help to how what's
possible.

> Link everything: Make it possible to get from qplot to other pages that
> use it, or expand on it, or supplant it, or give examples for it…

I have tried this in the past in another project, and it's not as
helpful as you might think.  Links really need to be hand curated to
be useful - that's the job of the see also section.

> Link to stack overflow, and crossvalidated, and to bloggers who’ve used
> the package and tried to give good specific examples.

I think that's a great idea, but I don't have that list...

> Have a search box which aggregates stackoverflow, r-help with tags for
> ggplot2…

I think that's getting beyond the scope of the documentation.

> Negative comments
> This alphabetical list of  250+ functions will not help people trying to
> learn ggplot or solve a problem
> Probably doesn’t need to have a dedicate dbox of dependencies, etc. Maybe
> this whole page could be an appendix: an alphabetical listing and technical
> data?
> The top link of "ggplot2-package: ggplot2” takes you to this:
>
>
>
>
>

> I think at that point most people will give up (some will cry :-) )

Well, that's one of the documentation pages that needs the most work.
Patches are welcome.

> Take this with a grain of salt, I’ve just been teaching  in R with bright
> post-graduates highlights and it drives home repeatedly to me how they see R
> as almost purposively obscure and inconsistent during their learning
> (despite their also loving how R gets things done when it does work smoothly
> for them)

Yes, but you can't learn R from the documentation! You have to
internalise a few organising principles first, and the documentation
(which is very task driven) is not appropriate.

> There’s also a _very_ low bar set for help R in general, with error
> messages that help you solve the error frowned upon.

Writing good error messages is surprisingly hard - you need to be able
to build up an accurate mental model of what the user might have done
to trigger the error, and what is going to help them fix it.

> Compare to a well organized and helpful site, like
>  http://www.statmethods.net
>
> I think he went backwards with the reworking, but it is still a great
> place to learn R from.

But a bad place to look up the specifics of individual functions.

> My guess is that if you stick a markdown wiki into had.co.nz <http://had.co.nz>, then users
> can take care of all of this for you: many of us like to store knowledge
> publicly.

As Brian mentioned, there already is a markdown wiki.  I personally
doubt that a wiki can ever make an excellent learning resource because
it lacks the single vision needed to make an effective, linear,
learning experience.  The other problem with the wiki is maintenance -
it's easy to dump some code up on a wiki, but it's much hard to keep
it working for 5 years.  One of the reasons that incorporating code
into ggplot2 takes longer than might be expected is that I have to be
able to make a long-term commitment to maintain it - and this means it
needs to be clear and well-written.

Hadley

Department of Statistics / Rice University

messages.subject: geom_raster and embedFonts
messages.body_plain: I usually output graphics from ggplot as PDF and then embed nicer-than-unspecified-helvetica fonts using the embedFonts function, which runs a suitable ghostscript command through system to embed the fonts. I've been experimenting with geom_raster, which in general seems very nice and seems to solve the hairline border issue with geom_tile, but after embedFonts, the PDF comes out as a mess: the raster surface seems blurred and appears black and white in Adobe Reader while Sumatra shows the originals colors. Does anyone know what happens here? Is there a magic gs option that will make the problem go away? Or is there another not-routed-through-LaTeX way to embed fonts in a PDF?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Some weeks ago I wrote a own little script (which will hopefully end in a R-package) which includes a ggplot2 function. Now after updating to the new ggplot2 version I run into an error with this function but I am unsure what is causing it. Here the function in my code:

# Plot commands to ggplot2
pdk <- ggplot(tmp, aes(x=x, y=y))+
	stat_function(fun=eq_lwr,aes(colour="lower/upper bound"),n=500)+
	stat_function(fun=eq_upr,aes(colour="lower/upper bound"),n=300)+
	stat_function(fun=eq_fit,aes(colour="fitted mean"),size=0.8,n=300)+
	scale_y_continuous("Probability",limits=c(0,eq(0,fishmove$pred.fishmove["fit","sigma_stat",,,,],fishmove$pred.fishmove["fit","sigma_mob",,,,],p)))+
	scale_x_continuous("Movement Distance (m)")+
	scale_colour_manual("",c("fitted mean"="green4","lower/upper bound"="grey65"))+
	theme_bw()+
	opts(	legend.position = c(0.95,0.85),
					legend.justification ="right",
					legend.title = theme_blank(),
					legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 'grey', fill = 'white'),
					panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
					title = fishmove$call)

The error says: Error in scale$palette(n) : argument "values" is missing, with no default
Calls: print ... FUN -> scale_map -> scale_map.discrete -> <Anonymous>
Execution halted

In the old version appropriate values for the scales where set automatically.
How is that handled in the new version? What do I need to add/change in my code?

Maybe anyone can help me! Thank you very much,

best regards,

/johannes

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
messages.body_plain:
The suggestion about pay for answers will not substitute the ggplot2 list in my point of view.

I'm very new with ggplot2 and this list, but on those some months I had seen some amount of messages of users who just want to create some nice-looking graphs, and had just landed on the R and ggplot world, having basic primary questions about ggplot2 and R itself.

The paid system could aim this kind of user, where the time to see the graph working is important enough to pay for, and the study and comprehension of ggplot and R can come later.

With this, the workflow will be answer first the pending "paid" questions, offering a complete full solution covering ggplot2 and R code, and after keep helping on the "open" list.

Complete full solution on the "open" list will not disappear, will just take some more time to shows up, because the "priority" of the paid questions.

And a suggestions: the paid solutions could be later accessible to everyone in the form of tutorials or something like. What do you think?

>> Negative comments

>> learn ggplot or solve a problem
>> Probably doesn’t need to have a dedicate dbox of dependencies, etc. Maybe
>> this whole page could be an appendix: an alphabetical listing and technical
>> data?
>> The top link of "ggplot2-package: ggplot2” takes you to this:
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> I think at that point most people will give up (some will cry :-) )

IF one wanted to provide a little more guidance to users visiting with multiple purposes/hopes/skill levels, perhaps something between automatically generated documentation and the book, there could be a static piece that gives some hints.  I have had some success with undergraduates by asking them to think about their data first, then leading them to appropriate types of plots to make.   For instance (word choice here is not what I would use, nor is this a good structure to use):

Is your data univariate?  Consider the following types of plots (geoms)...
Is your data bivariate?  Consider...
Is your data continous or discrete?
Do you want to group by some factor/category?

One could construct a (somewhat) dichotomous key or other mechanism that leads to suggested ggplot examples, and introduces the total newbie to the ggplot conceptual vocabulary (geoms, faceting etc).  I used to have a web site that did this using base and lattice graphics, before I learned ggplot.  Never really fleshed out the web site so I took it down, especially since I now always use ggplot for day to day plotting, and certainly in all my courses (where they gobble it up).

Bryan

Here is a more complete solution:

library(ggplot2)

info <- read.csv("info.csv",header=TRUE)

categories <- unique(info$category)

for (i in categories)
{
  plot_data <- subset(info, category == i)
  qplot(x=x,y=y,data=plot_data, main=paste("Category of ",i,sep=""))
}

Where info is your data frame, loaded from a CSV file.

On 2012-Mar-21, at 14:43 , Ben Bond-Lamberty wrote:
>
> qplot(x, y, data = reg, type = "path",size=I(.5))    # or whatever 'size' you want; see ?geom_path

No the problem comes from the syntax itself, not the size argument. The type of geom is specified with the `geom` argument, not the `type` argument. So it should be:

library(maps)
library(ggplot2)
reg <- as.data.frame(map("world", plot = FALSE)[c("x", "y")])

qplot(x, y, data = reg, geom = "path")

In the previous example you were drawing points, which looked bigger.

The last line is exactly equivalent to what you did later:

ggplot(reg, aes(x, y)) + geom_path()

messages.subject: Re: Best practice
messages.body_plain:
I use word when I have to for clients and find that the metafile format works very well (also in FrameMaker, which I much prefer). I also insert the graphics as references to the file on disk rather than inserting the graphic to keep the word filesize reasonable. If it's necessary to resize the graphic, make sure to keep the aspect ratio the same as the original and you'll get a crisp figure at whatever size you need.

There is a caveat - if your figure has a lot of points/lines etc., it's often better to use a raster format created at the final size because word redraws the vector files every time you resize/scroll and this can cause annoying delays in editing. This is necessary also if you need transparent shading or lines as the metafile format doesn't support transparency in colors.

Finally, if you will create a pdf from the word file, be sure to use a pdf printer rather than the word 'save as pdf' feature because the word version messes up such things as rotation of labels, and some others, probably because MS wants you to use their pdf rival.

David Stevens

Hi,

Some thoughts....

Working in a big company, I can easily get for example USD900 for something that make sense to the company. It could be a file-area with all ggplot-material in one place, perhaps in the form of blog. I could argue that even if all the material is available on internet, I would save time. The ggplot book could be stored there too. This would be a voluntary model adapted to companies. I understand that T-shirts or cups are interesting, but in a corporate environments it can be difficult to ask for that. But to say "give me USD900 so I can save 10 hours per week" make sense to some managers. Honestly, at times I find it difficult to keep up with all great stuff people write about ggplot and R on blogs and forums, to have a structured place of getting the newest and best info, even if it is just links to open web-pages, would help a lot.

Best regards,
/Chris

messages.body_plain:
I'm plotting different variables in a faceted graph, and the variables have different scales. Is it possible for each graph to have its own color scale? m <- ggplot(nav.gg <http://nav.gg>,aes(lon_dd_r,lat_dd_r))

Kevin

messages.subject: geom_raster with partial data
messages.body_plain:
geom_raster seems to behave odd, when data is not a full rectangle. For example compare tiles and raster in the following

df = expand.grid(x=-10:10, y=-10:10)
df$z = rnorm(nrow(df))
df = subset(df, abs(x) + abs(y) > 15)
plot = (ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
        + geom_raster(aes(fill=z))
        + geom_tile(fill=NA, color="red", size=0.5)
        + coord_equal())

print(plot)

geom_raster seems to stretch the data to fill the gaps. Why? As a workaround I tried using NAs in the grid.

df = expand.grid(x=-10:10, y=-10:10)
df$z = rnorm(nrow(df))
df$z[abs(df$x) + abs(df$y) <= 15] = NA
plot = (ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
        + geom_raster(aes(fill=z))
        + coord_equal())

print(plot)

NAs are rendered with a grey color, but where is that color defined? I'd like to use white or alpha=0.

How do I use geom_raster with non rectangular or incomplete data?

messages.subject: Re: geom_raster with partial data
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Mar 22, 2012 at 6:54 AM, Osmo Salomaa <osmo.s...@strafica.fi> wrote:
> geom_raster seems to behave odd, when data is not a full rectangle. For
> example compare tiles and raster in the following
>
> df = expand.grid(x=-10:10, y=-10:10)
> df$z = rnorm(nrow(df))
> df = subset(df, abs(x) + abs(y) > 15)
> plot = (ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
>         + geom_raster(aes(fill=z))
>         + geom_tile(fill=NA, color="red", size=0.5)
>         + coord_equal())
>
> print(plot)
>
> geom_raster seems to stretch the data to fill the gaps. Why?

Because that's the way rasters work - they have to fill up the total
space you give them. If you reduce the number of pixels, each pixel
gets bigger.

> As a workaround
> I tried using NAs in the grid.
>
> df = expand.grid(x=-10:10, y=-10:10)
> df$z = rnorm(nrow(df))
> df$z[abs(df$x) + abs(df$y) <= 15] = NA
> plot = (ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
>         + geom_raster(aes(fill=z))
>         + coord_equal())
>
> print(plot)
>
> NAs are rendered with a grey color, but where is that color defined? I'd
> like to use white or alpha=0.

Try

plot + scale_fill_gradient(na.value = NA)

Hadley

--

Department of Statistics / Rice University

messages.body_plain:
Kevin,

Cool-looking data!

As far as I know--unless 0.9 has new capabilities in this
area--ggplot2 can't do what you want here. You have two options:
first, use viewport and set up multiple independent plots, each with
an independent color scale; second, rescale "value" so that they're
all in the same range, e.g.

nav.gg.rescaled <- ddply(nav.gg <http://nav.gg>,.(variable),function(d){d$value <-
rescale(d$value); d})

and then plot exactly as before. This puts the data (subsetted by
variable) on a common 0-1 scale.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: barchart help needed
messages.body_plain:
Dennis,
revisiting your code, I have another question.
obviously the figure sorted by category; how can the code make it sorted also then by weight?

thanks.
Jack

From: Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com>
To: Li Xiaobo <xiaobo...@yahoo.com>
Cc: Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com>; ggp...@googlegroups.com
Sent: Monday, June 20, 2011 6:48 PM
Subject: Re: barchart help needed

It always dawns on you two seconds after you post....

Re the alternative to the reshape() function, what I had in mind was,
for melting two or more *sets* of variables simultaneously, as in this
example,

data.frame(melt(test, id = c('Catergory', 'Product'),
                    measure = c('Rating', 'Weight')),
                    Count = melt(test, measure = c('ratingcount',
'weightcount'))$value)

Dennis

On Mon, Jun 20, 2011 at 3:38 AM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> Since you asked this on the ggplot2 list, it's only fair to give one
> ggplot2 solution. Josh did a great job showing you the lattice
> solution, which probably took a while, so I thought I'd pick up where
> he left off :) This isn't as trivial as it seems at first; the trick
> is to use geom_segment(), but that geom assumes a numeric x and
> numeric y, so we have to add a couple more variables to the mix. Just
> as an alternative, I show one way to get (almost) the same data frame
> as Josh's ltest using the reshape package's melt() function, although
> it's not quite as elegant as Josh's reshape() function solution, which
> is worth knowing BTW. [I've seen a way to do it with nested melt's
> before in this group, but I haven't hunted it down yet since I was
> occupied with the graph.]
>
> [I didn't add the CatCol column because it isn't necessary in ggplot2,
> but it is useful in the lattice call.]
>
> # Start with your data frame test:
> library(ggplot2)   # also loads reshape and plyr
>
> # Josh's definition for ordering levels of product by weight
> test$Product <- with(test, factor(Product,
>  levels = Product[order(Category, weight)]))
>
> # A useful function from the plyr package to rename variables
> # Would also be useful to rename 'Catergory' :)
> # You need to assign the result of rename(), otherwise it will just
> print and not keep the result
> test <- rename(test, c('weight' = 'Weight'))
>
> # Melt the data to combine Rating and Weight variables (to use as a
> facet variable)
> testa <- melt(test, id = c('Catergory', 'Product'),
>                     measure = c('Rating', 'Weight'))
>
> # Count stacks the ratingcount and weightcount variables, but
> # you need to make sure you have the right order...not 'safe'
> testa$Count <- with(test, c(ratingcount, weightcount))
>
> # Two new variables: a numeric version of Product and a numeric
> variable to define
> # the 'origin' of the bars for each variable
> testa$product <- as.numeric(testa$Product)
> testa$origin <- 100 * as.numeric(testa$variable == 'Weight')
>
> ## Base version of plot:
> g <- ggplot(testa, aes(x = product, y = value))
>
> g + geom_segment(aes(xend = product,
>                     yend = origin,
>                     colour = Catergory), size = 5) +
>    scale_x_continuous('Product', breaks = unique(testa$product),
>                        labels = levels(testa$Product)) +
>    theme_bw() +
>    ylab("Product\n") + xlab('Value') +
>    geom_text(aes(y = value + sign(value - origin), label = Count), size = 3) +
>    coord_flip() + facet_wrap(~ variable, nrow = 1, scales= 'free') +
>    scale_colour_manual(values = c('A' = 'purple', 'B' = 'blue', C= 'green')) +
>    opts(legend.position = 'none', title = "Weight and rating of all samples")
>
>
> It looks pretty much the same as the lattice graph, but keeps the
> guidelines. I also did a little work to space the locations of the
> count labels away from the bars.
>
> Dennis
>
>
> On Sun, Jun 19, 2011 at 10:08 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Hi Jack,
>>
>> You are using lattice, so I am not sure why you are posting to the
>> ggplot2 list (unless you wanted us to give you a ggplot2 solution?).
>> Anyway, I think the below might do what you want.  You should be able
>> to cut and paste into your console and run it.
>>
>> Hope this helps,
>>
>> Josh
>>
>> ###################  Code  ####################
>>
>> ## Read in your data
>> test <- read.table(textConnection("
>> Catergory,Product,weightcount,weight,ratingcount,Rating
>> A,A1,3,80,18,0.49
>> A,A2,2,99,38,-1.04
>> A,A3,5,98.8,47,4.59
>> A,A4,3,95.5,129,0.23
>> A,A5,5,90.8,64,-1.6
>> A,A7,1,94.1,4,-0.03
>> A,A6,4,90.1,114,-1.06
>> A,A8,3,97.2,75,-0.96
>> B,B1,2,91.2,21,0.32
>> B,B2,2,110,29,8.29
>> B,B3,5,93.4,170,1.46
>> B,B4,3,95,83,0.76
>> C,C1,1,88,6,0.6
>> C,C2,1,99.3,16,-3.75
>> C,C3,1,67.9,13,-0.27
>> C,C4,1,99,13,0.71
>> C,C5,1,87,15,-1.56
>> C,C6,2,94.2,19,-4.38
>> C,C7,1,96.8,6,0.91"), sep = ",", header = TRUE,
>>  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>> closeAllConnections()
>>
>> ## Convert 'Product' to a factor with levels ordered by
>> ## Catergory (alphabetically), then weight (numerically)
>> ## (btw, it is spelled "Category" not "Catergory")
>> test$Product <- with(test, factor(Product,
>>  levels = Product[order(Catergory, weight)]))
>>
>> ## Create a new variable with purple, blue, or green
>> ## depending on whether Catergory matches A, B, or C
>> test$CatCol <-
>>  c("purple", "blue", "green")[match(test$Catergory, c("A", "B", "C"))]
>>
>> ## look at the structure of the final data
>> ## I find it convenient to be consistent in my variable naming
>> ## scheme such as whether it is upper or lower case as this makes
>> ## it easier for me to remember what to type without checking
>> str(test)
>>
>> ## Convert data to long format so that conditioning can be used
>> ltest <- reshape(data = test, direction = "long", varying =
>>  list(c("weightcount", "ratingcount"),
>>       c("weight", "Rating")),
>>  v.names = c("Count", "Value"),
>>  times = c("weight", "rating"), timevar = "variable")
>>
>> ## look at the structure of the long data
>> str(ltest)
>>
>> require(lattice)
>>
>> ## create a both plots conditioning on the variable
>> ## note the addition of the scales argument to let the x axis
>> ## freely vary, and the slightly more complex specification of the origin
>> both.plots <- barchart(Product ~ Value | variable, data = ltest,
>>  stack = FALSE, rectangles = TRUE, horizontal = TRUE,
>>  ylab = "Product", xlab = "Value", col = ltest$CatCol,
>>  main = "Weight and Rating of all samples", border = "NA",
>>  scales = list(x = list(relation = "free")),
>>  panel = function(x, y, subscripts, ...) {
>>    panel.grid(h = 0, v = -1, col = "gray")
>>    panel.barchart(x, y, origin = ifelse(
>>      ltest$variable[subscripts][1] == "weight", 100, 0), ...)
>>    panel.text((x * 1.01), y,
>>      label = paste(ltest$Count[subscripts]),
>>      cex = 0.7)

geom_hline(yintercept=1,lt=2)+

messages.subject: Re: barchart help needed
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This line of code from Josh Wiley shows how the ordering was done:

test$Product <- with(test,
                     factor(Product, levels = Product[order(Category, weight)]))

It sorts the levels of Product by Category and then weight within
Category, so I'm rather confused about what you're asking, because it
seems to me that it's doing what you're requesting. If not, you should
describe in more detail what you want.

Dennis

On Thu, Mar 22, 2012 at 7:46 AM, Li Xiaobo <xiaobo...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> Dennis,
> revisiting your code, I have another question.
> obviously the figure sorted by category; how can the code make it sorted
> also then by weight?
>
> thanks.
> Jack
>
> From: Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com>
> To: Li Xiaobo <xiaobo...@yahoo.com>
> Cc: Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com>; ggp...@googlegroups.com
> Sent: Monday, June 20, 2011 6:48 PM
>
> Subject: Re: barchart help needed
>
> It always dawns on you two seconds after you post....
>
> Re the alternative to the reshape() function, what I had in mind was,
> for melting two or more *sets* of variables simultaneously, as in this
> example,
>
> data.frame(melt(test, id = c('Catergory', 'Product'),
>                     measure = c('Rating', 'Weight')),
>                     Count = melt(test, measure = c('ratingcount',
> 'weightcount'))$value)
>
> Dennis
>
> On Mon, Jun 20, 2011 at 3:38 AM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Hi:
>>
>> Since you asked this on the ggplot2 list, it's only fair to give one
>> ggplot2 solution. Josh did a great job showing you the lattice
>> solution, which probably took a while, so I thought I'd pick up where
>> he left off :) This isn't as trivial as it seems at first; the trick
>> is to use geom_segment(), but that geom assumes a numeric x and
>> numeric y, so we have to add a couple more variables to the mix. Just
>> as an alternative, I show one way to get (almost) the same data frame
>> as Josh's ltest using the reshape package's melt() function, although
>> it's not quite as elegant as Josh's reshape() function solution, which
>> is worth knowing BTW. [I've seen a way to do it with nested melt's
>> before in this group, but I haven't hunted it down yet since I was
>> occupied with the graph.]
>>
>> [I didn't add the CatCol column because it isn't necessary in ggplot2,
>> but it is useful in the lattice call.]
>>
>> # Start with your data frame test:
>> library(ggplot2)   # also loads reshape and plyr
>>
>> # Josh's definition for ordering levels of product by weight
>> test$Product <- with(test, factor(Product,
>>  levels = Product[order(Category, weight)]))
>>
>> # A useful function from the plyr package to rename variables
>> # Would also be useful to rename 'Catergory' :)
>> # You need to assign the result of rename(), otherwise it will just
>> print and not keep the result
>> test <- rename(test, c('weight' = 'Weight'))
>>
>> # Melt the data to combine Rating and Weight variables (to use as a
>> facet variable)
>> testa <- melt(test, id = c('Catergory', 'Product'),
>>                     measure = c('Rating', 'Weight'))
>>
>> # Count stacks the ratingcount and weightcount variables, but
>> # you need to make sure you have the right order...not 'safe'
>> testa$Count <- with(test, c(ratingcount, weightcount))
>>
>> # Two new variables: a numeric version of Product and a numeric
>> variable to define
>> # the 'origin' of the bars for each variable
>> testa$product <- as.numeric(testa$Product)
>> testa$origin <- 100 * as.numeric(testa$variable == 'Weight')
>>
>> ## Base version of plot:
>> g <- ggplot(testa, aes(x = product, y = value))
>>
>> g + geom_segment(aes(xend = product,
>>                     yend = origin,
>>                     colour = Catergory), size = 5) +
>>    scale_x_continuous('Product', breaks = unique(testa$product),
>>                        labels = levels(testa$Product)) +
>>    theme_bw() +
>>    ylab("Product\n") + xlab('Value') +
>>    geom_text(aes(y = value + sign(value - origin), label = Count), size =
>> 3) +

messages.subject_clean: Ordering bars in bar charts with 2 layers in ggplot2 0.9?
messages.body_plain:
For me it looks the same in ggplot2 0.8.9 and 0.9.0 -- they bars are in order without subset, but they're out of order with subset. My guess is that this is happening because ggplot is dropping the unused factor levels from each subset, then, when it puts the subsets back together, it recomputes the factor levels naively, so they get sorted alphabetically.

For me, using scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) fixes the problem.

set.seed(124)

MyData <- data.frame(
 measurement = runif(10, min=-1, max=1),

 site        = letters[1:10]
)

# Order the levels of site, by values of measurement
MyData$site <- reorder(MyData$site, MyData$measurement)

# Bars in order
ggplot(MyData, aes(site, y=measurement)) + geom_bar()

# Bars not in order (with subset)
ggplot(MyData, aes(site, y=measurement)) +
  geom_bar(subset = .(measurement < 0)) +
  geom_bar(subset = .(measurement >= 0))

# Bars in order
ggplot(MyData, aes(site, y=measurement)) +
  geom_bar(data = subset(MyData, measurement < 0)) +
  geom_bar(data = subset(MyData, measurement >= 0)) +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE)

-Winston

R will do xsplines which given the correct arguments will give close
approximations to Bezier curves.  There may be a way to use
grid.xspline to plot an xspline in a ggplot function, or you can use
the xspline function with draw=FALSE to get the xy points to
approximate the spline, then use ggplot functions to draw the path
through these points.

messages.body_plain:
OK, as it turns out, the problem stemmed from a change to the themes
syntax.  The actual code that we were using to generate plots called a
"my_theme()", which was based on "theme_bw()".  Previously, themes
used "NA", as in these lines:

            legend.key.height = NA,
            legend.key.width = NA,

But in the latest version of ggplot, NAs are no longer OK it appears
because as soon as I changed those lines to the following, everything
worked:

            legend.key.height = NULL,
            legend.key.width = NULL,

Very frustrating that upgrading ggplot led to so much downtime and
hair-pulling for people in my lab this week.

Matthew

my_theme<- function (base_size = 12, base_family = ""){
    structure(
        list(
            axis.line = theme_blank(),
            axis.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "black", vjust = .5),
            axis.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "black", hjust = .5),
            axis.ticks = theme_segment(colour = "grey50"),
            axis.title.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size, vjust = -1),
            axis.title.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size, angle = 90, vjust = 0),
            axis.ticks.length = unit(0.15, "cm"),
            axis.ticks.margin = unit(0.1, "cm"),
            legend.background = theme_rect(colour = "white"),
            legend.key = theme_rect(fill = "white", colour = "white"),
            legend.key.size = unit(1.2, "lines"),

            legend.key.height = NA,
            legend.key.width = NA,

            legend.text = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8),
            legend.text.align = NA,
            legend.title = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
            legend.title.align = NA,
            legend.position = "right",
            legend.direction = "vertical",
            legend.box = NA,
            panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "grey90", colour = NA),
            panel.border = theme_blank(),
            panel.grid.major = theme_line(colour = "white"),
            panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour = "grey95", size = 0.25),
            panel.margin = unit(0.25, "lines"),
            strip.background = theme_rect(fill = "grey80", colour = NA),
            strip.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8),
            strip.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size =
base_size * 0.8, angle = -90),
            plot.background = theme_rect(colour = NA, fill = "white"),

base_size * 1.2, vjust = 1.5),

    )
}

messages.body_plain:
Karin,

 > that I need to reshape my data somehow before proceeding

Yes, you were on the right track. Try the code below, which takes the
data you provided, uses 'melt' to reshape it into a useful form, and
then makes two plots following your guidelines.

Ben

library(ggplot2)
library(reshape)

data <- structure(list(Name = structure(c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("a1",
"a2"), class = "factor"), Aha1 = c(0L, 1L, 0L, 3L), Aha2 = c(3L,
4L, 0L, 0L), Aha3 = c(3L, 4L, 4L, 5L), Aha4 = c(4L, 0L, 0L, 0L
), Total = c(11L, 11L, 5L, 10L), Group = structure(c(1L, 2L,
1L, 2L), .Label = c("01", "16"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("Name",
"Aha1", "Aha2", "Aha3", "Aha4", "Total", "Group"), row.names = c(NA,
-4L), class = "data.frame")

mdata <- melt(data,id.vars=c("Name","Group","Total"))

for( i in levels(mdata$Name)) {
	d <- droplevels(subset(mdata,Name==i & value>0))
	p <- ggplot(d,aes(variable,value/Total*100))
	print(p+geom_bar(stat="identity",position="dodge")+opts(title=i))
	readline("<Return>")
}

messages.subject: Re: reverse palette colors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fred -

The below works easily, although I'm sure there's a way to do it directly from scale_fill_brewer.

m <- read.csv('example.csv')
a <- cut(m$var.eff.size, 5)

bin <- .25*(1:3)
xi <- quantile(m$effect.size, bin)
qplot(effect.size, data = m, geom = 'histogram',
    fill = a, main = 'Frequency Distribution') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xi) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'e', y = 'f', fill = 'e') +
  scale_fill_brewer(type = 'seq')

# straight reversal
fills <- rev(brewer.pal(5, 'Blues'))
qplot(effect.size, data = m, geom = 'histogram',
    fill = a, main = 'Frequency Distribution') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xi) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'e', y = 'f', fill = 'e') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fills)

# darker
fills <- rev(brewer.pal(7, 'Blues'))[1:5]
qplot(effect.size, data = m, geom = 'histogram',
    fill = a, main = 'Frequency Distribution') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xi) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'e', y = 'f', fill = 'e') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fills)

# in general
fills <- c('red','green','blue','purple','orange')
qplot(effect.size, data = m, geom = 'histogram',
    fill = a, main = 'Frequency Distribution') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xi) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'e', y = 'f', fill = 'e') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fills)

Cheers
david.

PS - nice to see ggplot2 has made it into the Psych department at Rice!

messages.subject: add median/mean to violin/boxplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!
This is my first post on ggplot2.

I am trying to add the mean to a violin/boxplot graphic. When I have
only one factor it is working fine but when I have two factors the
mean of each factor appears only in the middle (not in the box or
violin plots). I played with alpha and width with no luck. My second
problem is that the boxplots are not inside the violin plots.

Any help would be really appreciated.
martin

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(plyr)

A reproductible example (data=test in the code below):

structure(list(Site = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
2L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label =
c("Site1",
"Site2", "Site3"), class = "factor"), Treatment = structure(c(1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("Control", "test"), class = "factor"),
    Value = c(4L, 3L, 11L, 22L, 6L, 7L, 3L, 9L, 6L, 10L, 20L,
    30L, 40L, 2L, 4L, 5L, 8L, 10L, 21L, 30L, 2L, 5L, 8L, 10L,
    3L, 4L, 5L, 6L, 7L, 8L, 22L, 21L, 20L, 14L, 5L, 3L)), .Names =
c("Site",
"Treatment", "Value"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-36L))

My code:
ggplot(test, aes(Site, Value)) + geom_violin(aes(fill=Treatment))
+ geom_boxplot (aes(fill=Treatment), alpha=1, width=0.5) + ylim(0,50)
+ opts(legend.position=c(0.1,0.7)) + opts(axis.title.x =
theme_blank())
+ stat_summary(aes(group=Treatment), fun.y=mean, geo="point",
fill="black", shape=21, size=3)

messages.subject: Re: plot inside a for loop
messages.body_plain:
You need to wrap the last line that constructs your graph (which I think is the whole loop body for you) in print() to trigger the actual plotting. When you do this interactively the REPL automatically prints, but that's turned off inside the loop mechanism.

Canonical answer: see R FAQ 7.31

Hope that helps,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
I think this is a rigged version of what you want, I'm sure Winston will have a better solution :

ggplot(aes(x = Site, y = Value), data = test) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill=Treatment), alpha = .25) +
  geom_boxplot (aes(fill=Treatment), alpha=.25, width=0.5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  stat_summary(aes(group=Treatment), fun.y=mean, geom="point",
    fill="black", shape=21, size=3, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  ylim(0,50) +
  opts(
    legend.position=c(0.1,0.7),
    axis.title.x = theme_blank()
  )

Strangely,  the following doesn't work (it only moves one of the groups, and not both).  It may be a bug...

w <- .2
ggplot(aes(x = Site, y = Value), data = test) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill=Treatment), alpha = .25, position = position_dodge(width = w)) +
  geom_boxplot (aes(fill=Treatment), alpha=.25, width=0.5, position = position_dodge(width = w)) +
  stat_summary(aes(group=Treatment), fun.y=mean, geom="point",
    fill="black", shape=21, size=3, position = position_dodge(width = w)) +
  ylim(0,50) +
  opts(
    legend.position=c(0.1,0.7),
    axis.title.x = theme_blank()
  )

You can probably get what you want from there.

Cheers
david.

messages.subject: Annotation_raster does not work with scale_x_reverse
messages.subject_clean: Annotation_raster does not work with scale_x_reverse
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've already posted this issue on stackoverflow, but I didn't get any
response so far
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9802936/annotation-raster-does-not-work-with-scale-x-reverse
I suspect it may be a bug, but I'm not sure whether it should better
be reported to the github pages.

I'm creating geographic maps with raster files as background. For
better display I want to flip some of them sidewards (i.e. so that
north points to the left, instead of up). This means that I have to
reverse the x-axis (in addition to flipping x and y), because
otherwise the data are displayed wrongly (mirrored).

It works with geom_tile, but of course this is very slow, especially
when doing facets. So, I want to use annotation_raster. This works
fine as well, but only until I reverse the x-axis. Then it is not
displayed any more.

In addition and I suspect that this may be related: swiching xmin and
xmax values doesn't seem to have any effect. Always displays with
xmin=min(xmin,xmax) and xmax=max(xmin,xmax).

library(ggplot2) ## v0.9.0

## works
qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars) +   annotation_raster(rainbow, xmin=15,
xmax=20, ymin=3, ymax=4)

## swiching xmin and xmax, doesn't affect plotting
qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars) +   annotation_raster(rainbow, xmin=20,
xmax=15, ymin=3, ymax=4)

## doesn't work
qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars) +   annotation_raster(rainbow, xmin=15,
xmax=20, ymin=3, ymax=4) + scale_x_reverse()

Cheers
Benschee

messages.subject: annotate "rect" in new ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in an older script I used following lines to expand the y-axis and to add a
grey rectangle manually to a plot (to make a similar look like facett plots).
The following lines were working before (I can't remember if in the dev-mode or the normal mode) but in the new version, no rectangle is plotted...

y <- runif(1000,1,50000)
x <- runif(1000,1,10)

df <- data.frame(x,y)
yrange <- c(0.01,1000000)

ggplot(df, aes(x=x,y=y))+
		geom_point()+

messages.subject: Legend above title in 0.9.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi, ggploteRs,

I just upgraded to 0.9.0 and noticed a change I cannot fix. If I place a horizontal legend above the plot (legend.position = "top") it's placed above the title instead of below. Anyway to reverse the order? I.e. legend below the title. Here's some code. Attachments show the difference between 0.8.9 and 0.9.0.

library(ggplot2)
sessionInfo()
ggplot.ver <- packageVersion("ggplot2")

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg))
p <- p + geom_point(aes(colour = qsec))
p <- p + opts(title = ggplot.ver,
              legend.position = "top",
              legend.direction = "horizontal")

filename <- paste("legend_", ggplot.ver, ".png", sep = "")
png(filename)
print(p)
dev.off()

messages.subject: from pairs() to ggplot-scatterplot matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'd like to produce a scatterplot matrix where some of the axis should be log-scaled (and appropriately labeled) while others not.
Furthermore I'd like to show on one half of the matrix the dot plots (with a "trend" line) and on the other half the correlation factor r and its significane level.
So far I have done this plot with the function pairs() but I can't get it working to set log-scaled axis. Due to that and because all my other plot were made in ggplot I consider also to make this matrix-plot in ggplot. Does anyone has experience with scatterplot matrix plot including correlation results?

Here what I've done so far:

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor)
{
	usr <- par("usr"); on.exit(par(usr))
	par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
	r <- abs(cor(x, y))
	txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
	txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
	if(missing(cex.cor)) cex <- 0.5/strwidth(txt)

messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot users,

I am trying to create a box plot with smooth line with the code below, which was successful with a smaller dataset (example plot is below), but I got error when I used the same code but with a larger dataset.

p <- ggplot(d, aes(time, Resp)) + geom_boxplot()

p + facet_grid(.~trt) + geom_smooth(aes(group = 1))

The error message was:

Error in smooth.construct.cr.smooth.spec(object, data, knots) :

x has insufficient unique values to support 10 knots: reduce k.

So, I googled any help to solve this, and I came to R-help communication using below:

## summary function ##

stat_sum_single <- function(fun, geom="point", ...) {

   stat_summary(fun.y=fun, colour="red", geom=geom, size = 3, ...)

 }

stat_sum_df <- function(fun, geom="crossbar", ...) {

   stat_summary(fun.data=fun, colour="red", geom=geom, width=0.2, ...)

 }

## example from ggplot web page

c <- qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)

 c + stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", colour = "red")

c + stat_sum_single(mean, geom="line")

c + stat_sum_df("mean_cl_normal", geom = "smooth")

However, it seems to me it is not working if x-variable is factor.

#if cyl is factor?

c <- qplot(as.factor(cyl), mpg, data=mtcars)

c <- c + geom_boxplot()                             #creat box plot

 c + stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", colour = "red")

c + stat_sum_single(mean, geom="line")              #did't work

c + stat_sum_df("mean_cl_normal", geom = "smooth")  #didn't work

If I want to create a box plot overlay with smooth line (or mean line), in this case, x-variable should be factor variable. I also don’t know why  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1)) didn’t work (is there any way to reduce “knot”? ).

 Have anyone had the same problem? Any help would be appreciated.

Regards,

Kaori

           geom_boxplot() +

           stat_summary(fun.data = 'mean_cl_boot', colour = 'red', aes(x = as.factor(cyl)))

d + stat_sum_single(mean, geom = 'line', aes(x = as.numeric(as.factor(cyl))),
                           size = 3, colour = 'red')
d + stat_sum_df("mean_cl_normal", geom = "smooth", aes(x = as.numeric(as.factor(cyl))))

Hi there ggplot-Folks!

I'm quite new to "R" and "ggplot" and I have an issue regarding the legend editing. Here is my code. I know, it might not be that elegant it could be, but it works fine for me (but if you have any further suggestions - sharing them would be highly appreciated)

First of all I load my raw-data, which I gained from an RTCA-experiment:

library(gplots)
mcpd2<-read.xls("http://dl.dropbox.com/u/19497400/Data/20110929_raw_Caco2_copy.xls",sheet=1)

Now that I have my data, I've got to rename the columns:

colnames(mcpd2)<-c("Time",
                   "Hours",
                   "2M1000_A",
                   "2M1000_B",
                   "2M1000_C",
                   "2M0500_A",
                   "2M0500_B",
                   "2M0500_C",
                   "2M0250_A",
                   "2M0250_B",
                   "2M0250_C",
                   "2M0100_A",
                   "2M0100_B",
                   "2M0100_C",
                   "2M0050_A",

                   "2M0050_C",
                   "2M0025_A",
                   "2M0025_B",
                   "2M0025_C",
                   "2M0010_A",
                   "2M0010_B",
                   "2M0010_C",
                   "2M0001_A",
                   "2M0001_B",
                   "2M0001_C"
                   )

Now, I have to normalize to a certain timepoint by typing:

mcpd2.s<-
as.data.frame(
sweep(
data.matrix(mcpd2),
2,
data.matrix(mcpd2)[93,]
)
)

That done, I pick the concentrations I'd like to plot:

pick<-c("Time","01")

grep(
paste(
pick,
collapse="|"
),
colnames(mcpd2.s),

)
)

After that I melt the data obtained and make a colsplit with the reshape2-package:

  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,48))

+guides(fill=guide_legend(title="title"))

it just gives me a second legend with the desired title but doesn't replace the actual one. Also, the colors don't match with the graph and the legend items are not renamed. Am I missing something?

Any hint is highly appreciated.

Regards,
Falko

messages.subject: Re: editing legend items
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

First of all, thank you for the reproducible example.

Scales are one of the more difficult features of ggplot2 to master,
and a few things are going on here that you need to learn about:

  (i) You can define labels in a separate vector or as labels in a
factor() statement; since you want expressions, the former is
advisable in this case.
  (ii) When you map multiple aesthetics to the same variable and want
to use a single legend, you need to modify all legends with a suitable
scale_*() function, one for each aesthetic defined.
  (iii) You can modify a title either by picking a suitable variable
name for the factor of interest (which will be the default legend
title) or you can change it manually inside a scale_*() function.

Here's a way to get what I think you want with the legend:

# Create a factor variable for treatment rather than a character
variable so that you can control the ordering of the levels:
melt.M2$treat <- factor(melt.M2$Treat, levels = c('2M0001', '2M0010', '2M0100'))

# Create a list of expressions that can be passed into the scale
functions as the labels = argument:
labls <- list(expression(paste('1', mu, 'M', sep = "")),
               expression(paste('10', mu, 'M', sep = "")),
               expression(paste('100', mu, 'M', sep = "")))

ggplot(data = melt.M2, aes(x = Time, y = value, color = treat, fill = treat)) +
    stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal", geom="smooth", size=1, alpha=0.1) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 48)) +
    scale_color_manual('My title', breaks = levels(melt.M2$treat),
                                   values = c('blue', 'green', 'orange'),
                                   labels = labls) +
    scale_fill_manual('My title', breaks = levels(melt.M2$treat),
                                  values = c('blue', 'green', 'orange'),
                                  labels = labls)

Notice that both scale_color_manual() and scale_fill_manual() needed
to be used in order for the two legends to merge. More specifically,
the two legends need the same title, the same breaks, the same values
and the same labels for the merger to take place.

You don't need guide_legend() here unless you want to change aspects
of the legend that are under its control, which are described on its
help page.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It's not clear whether your binary variable is factor, character or
numeric, and it matters in terms of the specification given below.
Assuming it's numeric,

scale_color_manual('Flyer\nPromotion', values = c(0 = 'black', 1 = 'red'),
                              labels = c('No flyer', 'Flyer'))

If the variable is a factor, then you need something like

scale_color_manual('Flyer\,Promotion', breaks = levels(x$flyer),
                                  values = c('black', 'red'),
                                  labels = c('No flyer', 'Flyer'))

If it's character, then quote the 0 and 1 in the first statement.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: multiple plots/pdf without looping
messages.body_plain:
Irsan,

Here's one suggestion -- use dlply() from the plyr package.   dlply()
breaks a dataframe into pieces, applies a function to each piece, and
returns a list.   Please see simple example below.

Dave
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
require(plyr)
require(ggplot2)

plot.fn = function(df) {
  tstring = paste('Plot of vs =', df$vs[1])
  qplot(x=cyl,y=mpg, data=df, main=tstring) + facet_wrap('gear')
}

myplots = dlply(mtcars, ~vs, plot.fn)
typeof(myplots)
print(myplots)

messages.subject: Re: Histogram + xlimits
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Fri, Mar 30, 2012 at 2:41 PM, Filipe G Vieira
<fgarret...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear all,
>
> I've recently switched to ggplot2 and I must say that, so far, it has
> been pretty intuitive.
> However, I've encountered some problems when I try to limit the x-
> axis.
>
> Taking as an example this histogram:
> qplot(cyl,geom='histogram',data=mpg) + aes(fill=class)

Firstly, you're attempting to produce a stacked bar chart but trying
to use the histogram geom to produce it rather than geom_bar().
Secondly, a factor version of cyl would be more effective but you're
trying to fake it by making cyl continuous instead. Evidently, you
want the gap at 7, so one way to produce it is to create a factor
version of cyl whose levels range from 4 to 8 inclusive and then play
around a bit with scale_x_discrete() in conjunction with geom_bar():

mpg$cyl2 <- factor(mpg$cyl, levels = 4:8)
# Fails to insert the gap at 7 since there are no data at 7 (default action)
(p <- qplot(cyl2, geom = 'bar', data = mpg, fill = class))

# This trick using scale_x_discrete() produces the desired gap at 7:
p + scale_x_discrete(limits = as.character(levels(mpg$cyl2)))

# Contrast this with the following (same as first graph above):
p + scale_x_discrete(breaks = levels(mpg$cyl2))

# Equivalent specification:
# p + scale_x_discrete(breaks = as.character(levels(mpg$cyl2)))

There is a subtle but important distinction between limits and breaks
in discrete scales; unfortunately, this distinction is not well
documented at present so it's easy to miss. My first thought was to
use the latter expression, but it elided over cyl = 7 since it
contained no data to plot (this is documented in waiver()); I
serendipitously stumbled over the code I ended up using for the
desired graph.

# To eliminate the level corresponding to 4 cylinders, here is one way:
levels(mpg$cyl2)[-1]
p + scale_x_discrete(limits = as.character(levels(mpg$cyl2)[-1]))

>
> Just pointing out a minor issue, why aren't the bars centred around
> its x-axis label? I mean, the "5 cyl" bar is to the right of the x-
> axis 5 label, while the "6 cyl" bar is to the left of the label.

Because you're using a continuous scale for x and producing a
histogram whose endpoints are not such that the centers of the bins
line up the way you expected. This is why some of the bars are to the
left of a tick mark and others are to the right. The histogram
analogue of stacked bar charts is an area chart, but I doubt that
would look any better in this example or fix the difficulties you're
experiencing.

>
> - When I try to limit the x-axis:
> qplot(cyl,geom='histogram',data=mpg) + aes(fill=class) +
> scale_x_continuous(limits=c(5,8))
>
> The x-axis goes from 5 to 8 but I only get the "6 cyl" bar!! Why
> aren't the 5 and 8 cyl bars displayed?

Because the limits don't contain the portion of the bar to the left of
5 nor the portion of the bar to the right of 8 in your graph.

>
> - I tried using discrete scales:
> qplot(cyl,geom='histogram',data=mpg) + aes(fill=class) +
> scale_x_discrete(limits=c(5,8))

As shown above, scale_x_discrete() assumes that the set of potential
values is discrete rather than continuous. You actually get something
out of this code since mpg$cyl is integer, but it should have thrown
an error had mpg$cyl been numeric.

I can sympathize with your angst because learning how to produce
customized positional axis and legend guides is an acquired skill; it
was the part of ggplot2 I had the most trouble getting my head around
when first learning it.

>
> but I get all bars with just the 5 and 8 cyl label!!!!
>
> - Tried stating all labels:
> qplot(cyl,geom='histogram',data=mpg) + aes(fill=class) +
> scale_x_discrete(limits=c(5,6,7,8))
>
> but I still get all bars (although with corrected labels)

Histograms are designed for continuous x scales and bar charts for
discrete x scales (typically factors), but there is some fuzziness in
how they are rendered in ggplot2.

>
>
>
> What do I have to do to have this histogram plotted with just the bars
> from 5 to 8??

I guess the first step would be to recognize the distinction between a
bar chart and a histogram; you want the former in this case.

HTH,
Dennis
